The *RES section of `*D_NET n71`, driven by u1:ZN, lists (index, node, node, value): 5 n71:4 u4:A 0.049; 6 n71:1 u7:B 0.018; 3 n71:2 n71:3 0.073; 1 u1:ZN n71:1 0.017; 4 n71:3 n71:4 0.013; 2 n71:1 n71:2 0.038. What is the series resistance from the driver u1:ZN to the sink u4:A, in ohms?
problems.e: Follow the chain u1:ZN through n71:1 ... n71:4 to u4:A, skipping the branch to u7:B, and scale by the R unit: 190 ohms.

problems.q: A SPEF file declares `*R_UNIT 1 KOHM`. The *RES section of `*D_NET n522`, driven by u1:ZN, lists (index, node, node, value): 1 u1:ZN n522:1 0.09; 2 n522:1 n522:2 0.02; 4 n522:3 n522:4 0.042; 6 n522:5 u4:A 0.077; 3 n522:2 n522:3 0.086; 5 n522:4 n522:5 0.064; 7 n522:3 u7:B 0.052. What is the series resistance from the driver u1:ZN to the sink u4:A, in ohms?
problems.e: Follow the chain u1:ZN through n522:1 ... n522:5 to u4:A, skipping the branch to u7:B, and scale by the R unit: 379 ohms.

label: GDSII stream records
lesson:
# GDSII stream records

GDSII is the binary stream format in which layouts reach the mask shop, and KLayout, Magic and every DRC engine read and write it. Unlike LEF and DEF it is a flat sequence of typed binary records, so a reader is a loop over record headers. Knowing the record layout lets a tool designer size files, write a minimal reader, and convert stored integers into physical coordinates.

## Record headers and the XY record

Every GDSII record starts with a 4-byte header: a 2-byte big-endian length that counts the whole record including the header, a 1-byte record type (HEADER, BGNLIB, UNITS, BGNSTR, BOUNDARY, XY, ENDEL and so on) and a 1-byte data type (no data, 2-byte integer, 4-byte integer, 8-byte real, ASCII string). A reader reads the header, then length minus 4 bytes of payload, and dispatches on the type. Coordinates live in XY records as pairs of 4-byte signed integers, 8 bytes per point. A BOUNDARY is closed by repeating its first point, so a rectangle with 4 vertices stores 5 points: $4 + 8 \times 5 = 44$ bytes. An L-shaped polygon with 6 vertices stores 7 points, $4 + 56 = 60$ bytes.

## Bytes in a layout element

An element is a sequence of records ending in ENDEL. A BOUNDARY element is BOUNDARY (4 bytes, no data), LAYER (4 + 2), DATATYPE (4 + 2), XY (4 + 8(n + 1)) and ENDEL (4), so an n-vertex boundary costs $24 + 8(n + 1)$ bytes: 64 bytes for a rectangle. A PATH element is a wire with a centerline: PATH, LAYER, DATATYPE, WIDTH (4 + 4, a 4-byte integer), the XY of its k points (not closed, so no repeated point) and ENDEL, which is $28 + 8k$ bytes. A structure holding two rectangles and a 3-point path is $64 + 64 + 52 = 180$ bytes. Sizes like these explain why flat GDS of a large chip runs to many gigabytes, and why hierarchy, with SREF and AREF references to shared structures, and the more compact OASIS format matter.

## Database units to microns

Coordinates are integers in database units. The UNITS record holds two 8-byte reals: the size of a database unit in user units, and its size in meters. A typical library stores 0.001 and 1e-9: one database unit is 1 nm, and the user unit is the micron. An XY integer of 123456 is then $123456 \times 10^{-9}$ m $= 123.456$ um. With a database unit of 5e-10 m the same integer is 61.728 um. A reader must use the meter value, not assume nanometers, and a tool that merges GDS files from different sources, as the final step of a flow merges cell GDS into the design, must rescale any file whose database unit differs, or reject it. The 8-byte reals use the GDSII excess-64 base-16 floating-point format, not IEEE 754, which a hand-written reader must decode explicitly.

## Going deeper

The GDSII Stream Format manual (Calma, release 6.0); the KLayout documentation on stream formats.

problems.q: A GDSII writer emits a BOUNDARY for a U-shaped polygon with 8 distinct vertices. Every record starts with a 4-byte header (2-byte length that includes the header, 1-byte record type, 1-byte data type), each coordinate is a 4-byte signed integer, and a boundary repeats its first point to close. How many bytes long is the XY record?
problems.e: The closed boundary stores 8 + 1 = 9 points, each an (x, y) pair of 8 bytes, plus the 4-byte header: 4 + 8 × 9 = 76 bytes.

problems.q: A GDSII writer emits a BOUNDARY for a L-shaped polygon with 6 distinct vertices. Every record starts with a 4-byte header (2-byte length that includes the header, 1-byte record type, 1-byte data type), each coordinate is a 4-byte signed integer, and a boundary repeats its first point to close. How many bytes long is the XY record?
problems.e: The closed boundary stores 6 + 1 = 7 points, each an (x, y) pair of 8 bytes, plus the 4-byte header: 4 + 8 × 7 = 60 bytes.

problems.q: A GDSII writer emits a BOUNDARY for a polygon with 20 distinct vertices. Every record starts with a 4-byte header (2-byte length that includes the header, 1-byte record type, 1-byte data type), each coordinate is a 4-byte signed integer, and a boundary repeats its first point to close. How many bytes long is the XY record?
problems.e: The closed boundary stores 20 + 1 = 21 points, each an (x, y) pair of 8 bytes, plus the 4-byte header: 4 + 8 × 21 = 172 bytes.

problems.q: Each GDSII record has a 4-byte header. A BOUNDARY element is the records BOUNDARY (no data), LAYER and DATATYPE (one 2-byte integer each), XY (closed, so the first point repeats; 8 bytes per point) and ENDEL (no data). A structure holds a 6-vertex boundary. How many bytes do these elements occupy?
problems.e: A boundary with n vertices costs 4 + 6 + 6 + (4 + 8(n + 1)) + 4 = 24 + 8(n + 1) bytes. The element sizes are 80, totalling 80 bytes.

problems.q: Each GDSII record has a 4-byte header. A BOUNDARY element is the records BOUNDARY (no data), LAYER and DATATYPE (one 2-byte integer each), XY (closed, so the first point repeats; 8 bytes per point) and ENDEL (no data). A structure holds a 4-vertex boundary and a 4-vertex boundary. How many bytes do these elements occupy?
problems.e: A boundary with n vertices costs 4 + 6 + 6 + (4 + 8(n + 1)) + 4 = 24 + 8(n + 1) bytes. The element sizes are 64 + 64, totalling 128 bytes.

problems.q: Each GDSII record has a 4-byte header. A BOUNDARY element is the records BOUNDARY (no data), LAYER and DATATYPE (one 2-byte integer each), XY (closed, so the first point repeats; 8 bytes per point) and ENDEL (no data). A PATH is PATH (4 bytes), LAYER, DATATYPE, WIDTH (header plus a 4-byte integer), XY with its points (an open path does not repeat a point) and ENDEL. A structure holds a 4-vertex boundary and a 3-point PATH with a WIDTH record. How many bytes do these elements occupy?
problems.e: A boundary with n vertices costs 4 + 6 + 6 + (4 + 8(n + 1)) + 4 = 24 + 8(n + 1) bytes. The element sizes are 64 + 56, totalling 120 bytes.

problems.q: A GDSII library's UNITS record holds the size of a database unit in user units, 0.01, and in meters, 1e-8. An XY coordinate stores the integer 847372. What is that coordinate in microns? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: One database unit is 1e-8 m = 0.01 um, so 847372 units are 8473.72 um.

problems.q: A GDSII library's UNITS record holds the size of a database unit in user units, 0.01, and in meters, 1e-8. An XY coordinate stores the integer 1548771. What is that coordinate in microns? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: One database unit is 1e-8 m = 0.01 um, so 1548771 units are 15487.71 um.

problems.q: A GDSII library's UNITS record holds the size of a database unit in user units, 0.0005, and in meters, 5e-10. An XY coordinate stores the integer 525061. What is that coordinate in microns? Round to 4 decimal places.
problems.e: One database unit is 5e-10 m = 0.0005 um, so 525061 units are 262.5305 um.

label: EDIF, IP-XACT, UPF and Si2 standards
prereqs: The map of design representations and formats
lesson:
# EDIF, IP-XACT, UPF and Si2 standards

Beyond Verilog, Liberty, LEF/DEF, SPEF and GDS, a tool meets a set of interchange standards for netlists, IP metadata and power intent. Each comes with its own syntax and its own parsing strategy: S-expressions, XML with a schema, or Tcl. Consortia such as Si2 steward several of them. A tool designer should recognize each format, know what it carries, and know what reader it needs.

## EDIF netlist interchange

EDIF (Electronic Design Interchange Format) describes netlists as nested S-expressions, LISP-style parenthesized lists: libraries contain cells, cells contain views, views have an interface (ports) and contents (instances and nets). One recursive reader can parse any EDIF file, because every construct is a list whose first element is a keyword. The price is verbosity: keywords repeat for every object. EDIF remains common in FPGA flows and older tool hand-offs. The parser's job is the same as for a Verilog netlist: build the same instances, nets and terminals in the object model. Importing the same design from EDIF and from Verilog should give identical connectivity, which is a cheap and powerful regression test for both readers.

## IP-XACT component metadata

IP-XACT (IEEE 1685) is an XML schema for describing IP blocks: components, bus interfaces with their port mappings, memory maps, address blocks and registers with their fields. It does not describe logic. It is the single source from which tools generate register RTL, C header files and documentation, and from which SoC integration tools wire blocks together by matching bus interfaces. A reader uses a standard XML parser and validates against the schema, rather than a hand-written grammar. A register of 32 bits with fields at bit offsets 0, 8 and 16 generates both the decode logic and the software mask constants, so hardware and software cannot drift apart.

## UPF power intent and the Si2 coalitions

UPF (Unified Power Format, IEEE 1801) captures power intent outside the RTL: `create_power_domain`, supply nets and ports, isolation, level shifting, retention and power states. Like SDC it is Tcl, so a tool reads it with a Tcl interpreter that defines these commands, and keeping it separate lets one RTL be implemented under different power strategies. Si2 (Silicon Integration Initiative) is an industry consortium whose member coalitions maintain standards, among them OpenAccess, a design database API, and the reference LEF/DEF parsers on which OpenDB's readers are based. Shared reference parsers matter because a format is only as standard as its corner cases: when tools share a parser, the same file means the same design to each of them.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1685 (IP-XACT); IEEE Std 1801 (UPF); the EDIF 2 0 0 specification; the Si2 OpenAccess documentation.

label: One database, many engines
prereqs: The RTL-to-GDSII flow end to end
lesson:
# One database, many engines

An EDA flow chains engines: floorplanner, placer, clock-tree builder, router, extractor, timer. They can be separate programs exchanging files, or modules of one program sharing one in-memory design database, as in OpenROAD. The choice shapes everything else: speed of optimization loops, how engines learn of each other's edits, and what can go wrong when they share state. Tool designers must know both architectures and their costs.

## Point tools that exchange files

In the classic architecture each step is a separate program. The placer writes DEF; the router reads it and writes routed DEF; the extractor writes SPEF; the timer reads Verilog, DEF, SPEF, Liberty and SDC. The formats are the contract, so any tool can be swapped for another vendor's. The cost is serialization at every boundary: a design with ten million instances may take minutes to write and parse, so a loop that wants timing feedback after every few thousand moves is impractical. A second cost is loss: anything the format cannot express, such as a tool-specific attribute, disappears in the round trip unless both sides agree on an extension.

## Engines on one in-memory database

OpenROAD links its engines into one application around OpenDB. Floorplanning, placement, resizing, CTS, routing, extraction and timing read and edit the same objects, so an engine's results are visible to the next immediately, with no file in between. This is what makes tight loops possible: the resizer swaps a master, the timer updates incrementally, and the resizer asks again, thousands of times. Each engine still keeps its own derived structures, such as the timer's graph with arrival times or the router's grid, built from the database. So sharing data creates a new duty: when one engine edits the database, every engine caching derived results must hear about it, typically through callbacks, and update incrementally.

## Consistency when engines share state

Shared mutable state brings classic hazards. If two engines edit concurrently without coordination, one can read a half-applied edit or corrupt a shared list, so tools allow one writer at a time, partition the design into regions, or use transactions. If the router deletes a wire while the timer holds a raw pointer to it, the timer crashes later; stable ids or handles, plus deletion callbacks, avoid that. Every path into the database must notify, including user Tcl edits; otherwise a manual change leaves the timer's cache stale and its next report wrong. Files do not disappear: shared-database tools still write DEF, Verilog and SPEF at stage boundaries as checkpoints and for hand-off to sign-off tools.

## Going deeper

Ajayi et al., "OpenROAD: Toward a Self-Driving, Open-Source Digital Layout Implementation Tool Chain" (GOMACTech 2019); the OpenROAD developer guide; the OpenDB documentation.

problems.a: Any tool can be swapped, because the formats are the contract between them
problems.e: Standard formats decouple tools. The cost is the serialization at every boundary.

label: Plug-in architectures
lesson:
# Plug-in architectures

Every long-lived EDA tool grows by extension: new synthesis passes, new placement penalties, new reports, new readers. A plug-in architecture lets that growth happen without editing the core. The patterns are old and simple, a registry, a factory and an interface, but the hard parts are the boundary itself: how plug-ins are built and loaded, and how the contract between host and plug-in survives change.

## Registries and factories

A registry maps a name to a way of constructing an implementation. Yosys shows the pattern: a pass is a C++ class derived from `Pass`, its constructor passes a name such as "my_opt" to the base class, and one static instance of the class is declared. Constructing that instance at start-up adds it to a global name-to-pass map, so typing `my_opt` in the shell finds and runs it. The same pattern serves policies inside an engine: a placer defines an abstract density-penalty interface, implementations register under names such as "bell", and a config file selects one by name. The core calls only the interface. Adding a penalty adds a registration, not a core edit. Duplicate names should be rejected, since silent replacement makes behavior depend on load order.

## Compiled-in modules versus loaded libraries

A plug-in can be compiled into the binary or loaded at run time. Yosys supports both: built-in passes, and shared libraries loaded with `yosys -m my_plugin.so`, whose static objects register their passes when the library loads. OpenROAD compiles its tools into one application, each module adding its Tcl commands at start-up. Compiled-in modules are built together, so they agree on the database layout, compiler and standard library; the price is a rebuild to add one. Loaded libraries can be added by users, but a C++ object crossing a library boundary depends on the C++ ABI: class layout, name mangling, standard-library types and exceptions. A plug-in built with another compiler version can compile cleanly and crash. A C-callable boundary passing plain structs and opaque handles is the robust choice.

## Versioning the plug-in contract

Once published, a plug-in interface is a promise. If the host adds a field in the middle of a struct, old plug-ins read wrong offsets. The defenses are standard: every struct carries a version or size field, fields are only appended, the plug-in declares the interface version it was built against, and the host checks it at load time so a mismatch is a clear error rather than a later crash. Plug-ins should keep no hidden global state, so instances run independently on many designs in parallel and results do not depend on scheduling. And the interface stays narrow: every function exposed is a function the core can never change freely again, so hosts expose a small, stable seam rather than their internals.

## Going deeper

The Yosys manual chapter on writing extensions; the OpenROAD developer guide on adding a tool; Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, "Design Patterns" (1994), on Factory Method and Abstract Factory.

problems.q:
What does a plug-in registry store per entry?

A) The plug-in's test results

B) A name and a way to construct the implementation (a factory)

C) A copy of the design database

D) The plug-in's source code
problems.a: A name and a way to construct the implementation (a factory)
problems.e: The registry maps names to constructors; the host creates instances on demand.

problems.q:
A Yosys pass is a C++ class whose constructor passes the name "my_opt" to the Pass base class, and one static instance is declared. How does `my_opt` become a command?

A) The user edits Yosys's main function

B) The static instance registers itself by name in a global registry at start-up

C) Yosys parses the C++ source at run time

D) The pass is found by scanning the file system
problems.a: The static instance registers itself by name in a global registry at start-up
problems.e: Self-registering objects are the classic plug-in pattern: constructing the instance adds it to a name-to-object map that the shell looks up.

problems.q:
A placer chooses a density penalty by name from a config file: "bell", "exponential" or "custom". Which pattern lets new penalties be added without editing the placer?

A) An abstract penalty interface plus a factory registry keyed by name

B) Copying the placer for each penalty

C) A global variable per penalty

D) A switch statement in the placer's core loop
problems.a: An abstract penalty interface plus a factory registry keyed by name
problems.e: The core calls the interface; the registry maps names to constructors. Adding a penalty adds a registration, not a core edit.

problems.q:
Yosys can load an extension with `yosys -m my_plugin.so`. What kind of plug-in is that?

A) A shared library loaded at run time that registers its passes

B) A Tcl script interpreted by Yosys

C) A Verilog module synthesized by Yosys

D) A pass compiled into the Yosys binary
problems.a: A shared library loaded at run time that registers its passes
problems.e: Dynamic loading lets users add passes without rebuilding Yosys; the loaded library's static objects register themselves.

problems.q:
Yosys can load an extension with `yosys -m my_plugin.so`. What kind of plug-in is that?

A) A Tcl script interpreted by Yosys

B) A Verilog module synthesized by Yosys

C) A shared library loaded at run time that registers its passes

D) A pass compiled into the Yosys binary
problems.a: A shared library loaded at run time that registers its passes
problems.e: Dynamic loading lets users add passes without rebuilding Yosys; the loaded library's static objects register themselves.

problems.q:
OpenROAD's tools (placement, CTS, routing) are compiled into one binary rather than loaded at run time. What does that choice buy?

A) One consistent build where all modules agree on the database and compiler

B) The ability to add tools without recompiling

C) Smaller memory use than any other design

D) Independence from the C++ ABI
problems.a: One consistent build where all modules agree on the database and compiler
problems.e: Compiled-in modules avoid ABI drift between separately built pieces; the price is that adding a module means rebuilding.

problems.q:
Why do tool vendors keep the plug-in interface small, even when users ask for access to internals?

A) Users cannot call more than ten functions

B) Small interfaces compile to faster code in every case

C) Large interfaces cannot be documented

D) Every exposed function becomes a promise that constrains future changes to the core
problems.a: Every exposed function becomes a promise that constrains future changes to the core
problems.e: A wide interface freezes internals. A narrow, stable one lets the core evolve behind it.

problems.q:
Why do tool vendors keep the plug-in interface small, even when users ask for access to internals?

A) Large interfaces cannot be documented

B) Every exposed function becomes a promise that constrains future changes to the core

C) Small interfaces compile to faster code in every case

D) Users cannot call more than ten functions
problems.a: Every exposed function becomes a promise that constrains future changes to the core
problems.e: A wide interface freezes internals. A narrow, stable one lets the core evolve behind it.

problems.q:
A host adds a field to the struct it passes to plug-ins. Old plug-ins now read the wrong offsets. What prevents this?

A) Renaming the struct

B) Recompiling the host only

C) Making all fields private

D) A version or size field in the struct, and adding fields only at the end
problems.a: A version or size field in the struct, and adding fields only at the end
problems.e: Versioned, append-only structs let old plug-ins keep working and let the host detect what each plug-in understands.

label: Database callbacks and observers
lesson:
# Database callbacks and observers

When engines share one design database, an engine that caches derived data, a timer's arrival times or a placer's density map, must learn when the design changes. The observer pattern does this: engines register callbacks with the database, and every edit notifies the subscribers. OpenDB provides this through callback objects attached to a block. The design questions are how many notifications an edit stream generates and how to keep their cost low.

## Observers subscribe to edit events

An observer registers for the kinds of edit it cares about. A timer cares about master swaps and pin connections, because both change delays and topology; a density map cares about moves and new instances; a global router cares about moves and connections. On each edit the database calls every observer subscribed to that kind. With a timer on {swap, connect}, a density map on {move, create} and a router on {move, connect}, the edit stream move, swap, connect, move costs $2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 7$ callbacks. Subscribing only to relevant kinds matters: an engine that subscribes to everything pays for every edit in the flow, and a million-move detailed placement then makes millions of useless calls.

## Mark dirty, recompute on query

A callback should be cheap. Recomputing timing inside every callback is ruinous when an optimizer makes thousands of edits between questions. Instead the observer records what changed, often just a dirty flag or a set of dirty objects, and recomputes when someone asks. For the session swap, move, swap, QUERY, connect, QUERY, QUERY with a timer subscribed to swap and connect, an eager timer recomputes 3 times, once per relevant edit. A lazy one recomputes at the first query (dirty from the two swaps), at the second (dirty from the connect), and not at the third (still clean): 2 times. The edits between queries are merged into one update, which is how incremental timers stay fast inside optimization loops.

## Batching notifications per transaction

Even cheap callbacks cost a function call and often a lock per edit. A database can batch: edits inside a transaction are collected, and at commit each observer that subscribed to at least one of them gets a single call carrying the list. With three transactions, if the timer is touched in all three and the density map in two, the batched cost is 5 calls, however many edits each transaction held. Batching also gives observers a consistent view: they never see a half-applied change such as an instance moved but not yet reconnected. The trade-off is latency, since an observer learns of an edit only at commit, and memory for the pending edit list.

## Going deeper

The OpenDB documentation on dbBlockCallBackObj; Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, "Design Patterns" (1994), the Observer pattern.

problems.q: A design database notifies registered observers on every edit: the timer subscribes to master swapped and pin connected or disconnected; the parasitic estimator subscribes to master swapped and pin connected or disconnected; the density map subscribes to instance moved, pin connected or disconnected and instance created; the power analyzer subscribes to instance moved. An optimizer then makes these edits in order: master swapped, instance created, instance created, master swapped, pin connected or disconnected, instance created. How many callback invocations does the database make in total?
problems.e: Each edit calls every observer subscribed to its kind: 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 1, which sums to 10.

An optimizer then makes these edits in order: pin connected or disconnected, pin connected or disconnected, master swapped, instance moved, pin connected or disconnected. How many callback invocations does the database make in total?
problems.e: Each edit calls every observer subscribed to its kind: 2 + 2 + 3 + 0 + 2, which sums to 9.

label: Incremental computation and dependency graphs
lesson:
# Incremental computation and dependency graphs

Every EDA tool caches derived results: parasitics computed from wires, delays from parasitics, arrivals from delays, slacks from arrivals. When the design changes, recomputing everything is too slow, and recomputing too little gives wrong answers. A dependency graph makes the cache honest. Each derived result is a node, each edge says which input it was computed from, and an edit tells the tool exactly which cached values may now be stale. This structure sits underneath incremental timing, incremental legalization and incremental builds alike.

## Invalidation follows forward edges

Draw an edge $u \to v$ whenever result $v$ is computed from $u$. The graph is acyclic, because no result can depend on itself, so it has a topological order. When an edit modifies node $u$, every node reachable from $u$ along edges may be stale, and no other node can be: its inputs are untouched. The invalid set is therefore the forward reachable set of the edited nodes, found by one depth-first or breadth-first search.

Example: edges $A \to B$, $A \to C$, $B \to D$, $C \to D$, $D \to E$ and $F \to E$. An edit to $B$ invalidates $D$ and $E$, two results; $A$, $C$ and $F$ keep their cached values. With several edits, the invalid set is the union of their reachable sets, so a result reachable from two edits is invalidated once, not twice.

## A query needs only its dirty ancestors

Invalidation is cheap; recomputation is the expensive part, and a lazy tool postpones it until someone asks. A query for node $q$ must bring $q$ up to date, and that requires every input of $q$ to be valid first, recursively. So the work for one query is the set of dirty nodes that are $q$ itself or ancestors of $q$. Dirty nodes elsewhere stay dirty.

Continuing the example, edit $B$ and then query $D$. The dirty set is $\{D, E\}$. The ancestors of $D$ are $A$, $B$ and $C$, all clean, so only $D$ is recomputed: one evaluation, although two results are dirty. A query for $E$ would recompute $D$ and then $E$. This is why a timer asked for the slack of one endpoint touches only that endpoint's fanin cone.

## Recompute in levels

When everything dirty must be refreshed, the topological order says what may run together. Give each dirty node a level: one more than the highest level among its dirty inputs, and 1 if all its inputs are clean. Nodes on the same level do not depend on one another, so a parallel engine can recompute a whole level at once, and the number of rounds equals the deepest level.

Example: edit $A$ in the graph above. Dirty nodes are $B$, $C$, $D$ and $E$. $B$ and $C$ have only the clean input $A$, so both are level 1. $D$ depends on $B$ and $C$, so level 2. $E$ depends on $D$ and the clean $F$, so level 3. Three rounds, the longest dirty path, however many workers there are. Long dependency chains limit incremental parallelism just as they limit full recomputation.

## Going deeper

Acar, "Self-Adjusting Computation" (PhD thesis, Carnegie Mellon, 2005); the Salsa and Adapton papers on demand-driven incremental computation; the OpenSTA source for how a timer tracks invalid arrivals.

label: Dirty flags and lazy invalidation
lesson:
# Dirty flags and lazy invalidation

A dirty flag is one bit per cached result that says "my inputs changed since I was computed." Setting flags is cheap, recomputing is not, and the gap between the two is where incremental tools win. An eager tool recomputes after every edit; a lazy one marks results dirty and recomputes only when a value is read. Combined with early cutoff, which stops propagation when a recomputed value comes out unchanged, dirty flags let an optimizer make thousands of edits between expensive queries.

## Eager recomputation after every edit

In the eager scheme, each edit immediately recomputes every result downstream of the edited node. The cost of a sequence of edits is the sum of the downstream set sizes, edit by edit, and results shared by several edits are paid for every time.

Example: edges $A \to C$, $B \to C$, $C \to D$, $D \to E$. A script edits $A$ and then $B$. Editing $A$ recomputes $C$, $D$ and $E$: three evaluations. Editing $B$ recomputes $C$, $D$ and $E$ again: three more. Total six. If the script makes $k$ edits that all feed the same cone of size $m$, eager evaluation costs $km$. Eager evaluation is simple and always leaves values valid, which is why it survives in small tools, but it scales badly when an optimizer makes many edits per query.

## Mark dirty, recompute on demand

In the lazy scheme, an edit walks forward and sets the dirty flag of every downstream result, stopping at results already dirty, since their descendants were flagged earlier. Nothing is recomputed until a read. A read of a dirty result first refreshes its dirty inputs, recursively, then clears the flag. If every result is eventually read once, each dirty result is recomputed exactly once.

For the same example, edits to $A$ and $B$ flag $C$, $D$ and $E$, the union of the two downstream sets. One query pass recomputes three results instead of six. In general lazy cost is the size of the union, eager cost the sum of the parts, and the saving grows with the overlap between edits. The price is that every read must check a flag, and code that reads cached fields directly, bypassing the check, silently returns stale data.

## Early cutoff on unchanged values

Dirty means "might have changed," not "has changed." When a result is recomputed and its new value equals the old one, its dependents see identical inputs and need no work. Early cutoff exploits this: re-evaluate a node only if at least one of its inputs actually changed value.

Example: edges $A \to B$, $B \to C$, $C \to D$, $A \to E$. An edit changes $A$, so $B$ and $E$ are re-evaluated. Suppose $B$ comes out unchanged, which happens in timing when the arrival at a pin is set by another, slower fanin. Then $C$ and $D$ are not re-evaluated, so only $B$ and $E$ are: two evaluations instead of four. A node reachable by another path that avoids $B$ is still re-evaluated. Cutoff needs a cheap equality test, which is one reason timers compare arrivals with a small tolerance rather than recomputing bit-exact values.

## Going deeper

Mokhov, Mitchell and Peyton Jones, "Build Systems à la Carte" (ICFP 2018), for dirty bits and early cutoff in build systems; the OpenSTA source for how it marks and refreshes invalid arrivals.

label: Incremental STA inside a tool
lesson:
# Incremental STA inside a tool

Inside an optimizer, a static timer is not a batch program that reads files and prints a report. It is a service living in the same process as the database, answering slack queries while the resizer, placer and router edit the netlist under it. Turning the timing-graph mathematics of incremental update into working software takes three pieces of infrastructure: a way to hear about edits, a way to record and refresh what they invalidate, and an understanding of which edits and queries are cheap.

## Edits reach the timer through callbacks

Tools that share one database learn about each other's edits through observers. The timer registers callbacks with the database; when an engine creates or deletes an instance, swaps its master, connects or disconnects a pin, or moves a cell, the database calls the timer before or after the change. The callback does not recompute timing. It updates the timer's own graph to match the database, adding or removing vertices and arcs, and it marks what is now stale: the delays of the affected arcs, the arrivals downstream and the required times upstream.

Callbacks must be fast, because a placement pass may produce tens of thousands of them. Recording "these pins are invalid" is constant work per edit; recomputing on each callback would multiply the cost of every edit by the size of a cone. Edits that change no electrical fact, such as renaming a net, should not invalidate anything.

## Invalidate, then propagate in level order

Invalidation splits into two directions. An arc change at $u \to v$ can change arrivals at $v$ and in its fanout cone, and required times at $u$ and in its fanin cone. A timer keeps separate invalid sets for the two, plus a set of arcs whose delays must be recalculated.

When a query arrives, the timer recomputes delays for invalid arcs, then processes invalid arrivals in increasing level order, so that every fanin is final before a pin's max is taken; required times are processed in decreasing level order. Two refinements matter. First, demand: a query for one endpoint's slack refreshes only its fanin cone and its own required time. Second, early termination: if a pin's new arrival equals its old one, its fanout need not be visited. OpenSTA implements this levelized lazy scheme; OpenTimer instead builds a task graph for the invalid region and runs it on a parallel task scheduler.

## What makes an incremental update expensive

Incrementality pays only when the changed region is small and the questions are local. Three patterns break it. A constraint edit, such as a new clock period or a changed input delay, alters required times at many endpoints, so the backward update can cover most of the design. A global query after every edit, such as asking for worst negative slack following each buffer insertion, forces a near-global refresh each time, so 10,000 edits cost 10,000 global updates. And structural edits that lengthen paths, such as inserting a buffer, can raise the levels of downstream pins, so level bookkeeping must itself be updated incrementally.

Good optimizer code batches edits, asks local questions (the slack of the endpoints it touched), and saves global summaries for checkpoints. A useful mental model: the cost of an update is the size of the region a query forces valid, not the size of the edit.

## Going deeper

The OpenSTA source and its documentation on network edits and incremental timing; Huang and Wong, "OpenTimer: A High-Performance Timing Analysis Tool" (ICCAD 2015) and the later OpenTimer 2 paper on task-based incremental timing.

label: Incremental legalization
prereqs: Rows, sites and the placement region
lesson:
# Incremental legalization

After global placement, a legalizer snaps every cell to a row and a site without overlap. During optimization, though, the design changes a little at a time: a resizer widens a cell, a buffer is inserted, a cell is moved. Re-legalizing the whole design for each change would scramble a carefully optimized placement and take far too long. Incremental legalization repairs only the neighbourhood of the change, moving as few cells as possible by as little as possible, which keeps timing and wirelength close to what the optimizer saw.

## Push-right shifting in a row

The simplest incremental repair works inside one row. Cells are kept sorted by x, each with a left edge $x_i$ and width $w_i$ in site units. When cell $k$ grows by $g$ sites with its left edge fixed, its right edge moves from $x_k + w_k$ to $x_k + w_k + g$. Walk right: each later cell must start at or after the right edge of its left neighbour, so its new position is $x'_i = \max(x_i,\ x'_{i-1} + w_{i-1})$. The walk stops changing anything at the first cell whose gap absorbs the push.

Example: cells at $x = 0$ (width 4), $x = 4$ (width 3), $x = 9$ (width 2) and $x = 11$ (width 5). Widen the first by 4. It now ends at 8, so the second moves to 8 and ends at 11. The third, at 9, must move to 11 and ends at 13. The fourth, at 11, moves to 13. Three cells move.

## Where a pushed cell lands

Each pushed cell lands exactly against its left neighbour, because the rule moves it by the least amount that removes the overlap. So positions in a pushed run are a running sum: the first pushed cell starts at the new right edge of the edited cell, and every following pushed cell starts at the right edge of the one before it, until a gap at least as large as the remaining push appears.

In the example, the pushed run is 8, 11, 13: the second cell at 8, the third at $8 + 3 = 11$, the fourth at $11 + 2 = 13$. Gaps before the edit were 0 between the first two cells, 2 between the second and third, and 0 between the third and fourth, so the push of 4 shrank to 2 after the first gap and stayed 2. A useful check: the shift of each pushed cell equals the push it received minus the gap in front of it.

## Total displacement and when to stop

The cost of an incremental repair is usually measured as total displacement, the sum of $|x'_i - x_i|$ over moved cells, because every moved cell perturbs its nets and the timing the optimizer just evaluated. In the example the shifts are 4, 2 and 2, a total of 8 sites.

Pushing in one direction is cheap but not minimal: a run might be better split, with some cells moving left into earlier gaps, which is what a dynamic-programming legalizer such as Abacus does when it re-solves the cluster positions that minimize quadratic displacement. A push can also run off the end of the row, and then cells must move to a neighbouring row. Production legalizers, such as OpenROAD's dpl, therefore search for nearby legal sites within a window and fall back to wider repairs only when a window has no room. The engineering rule is to bound the region touched, so the update stays local and the placement keeps its quality.

## Going deeper

Spindler, Schlichtmann and Johannes, "Abacus: Fast Legalization of Standard Cell Circuits with Minimal Movement" (ISPD 2008); the OpenROAD documentation for dpl (detailed placement).

label: Content-addressed result caching
prereqs: Expected value of a random variable
lesson:
# Content-addressed result caching

Flows recompute the same things over and over: a regression reruns unchanged designs, a parameter sweep shares its synthesis step, a developer reruns placement after editing only a report script. A result cache stores each step's output under a key computed from its inputs, so an identical invocation is answered by a lookup. The idea is the same one build systems use for object files. It is worth doing only when lookups are cheap relative to the computation, and correct only when the key covers every input that affects the output.

## Expected time with a cache

Let a lookup cost $L$ (hashing the inputs and probing the store), the computation cost $C$, and the hit rate be $h$. Every invocation pays the lookup; only misses pay the computation. The expected time is
$$E[T] = L + (1 - h)\,C.$$
Writing the result back into the store on a miss adds a little more, which we ignore here.

Example: an extraction step takes $C = 300$ s, the lookup costs $L = 12$ s and the hit rate is 75%. Then $E[T] = 12 + 0.25 \times 300 = 87$ s, against 300 s without a cache. The expectation is a linearity-of-expectation statement over many invocations; any single call takes either 12 s or 312 s. Large flows care about the expectation because they run thousands of steps.

## The break-even hit rate

A cache can lose. A miss costs $L + C$, more than the uncached $C$, so the cache helps on average only when
$$L + (1 - h)\,C < C \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h > \frac{L}{C}.$$
Example: hashing a large netlist and probing remote storage costs $L = 20$ s, and the step runs in $C = 160$ s. The break-even hit rate is $20/160 = 12.5\%$. Above it the cache saves time; below it, the cache is overhead.

The ratio $L/C$ explains where caching belongs. Long steps (synthesis, global routing, extraction) have tiny break-even rates and are excellent candidates. Short steps whose inputs are large (a quick report over a full database) may never pay back the cost of hashing their inputs. Cheap keys help: hashing file contents once and reusing the digest is far faster than rehashing on every lookup.

## Keys must hash every input

A content-addressed cache names a result by a hash of everything that determines it: the input files, the step's parameters, the random seed, and the version of the tool binary. Identical keys must mean identical outputs. If any determining input is missing from the key, two different computations share a key and the cache returns a wrong result, silently, which is far worse than a slow run.

Example: runs arrive with (netlist, SDC, tool version, seed) equal to (1, 1, 1, 2), (1, 1, 2, 2), (1, 1, 1, 2), (2, 1, 1, 1). The first, second and fourth keys are new and miss; the third repeats the first and hits, one hit. A key that omitted the tool version would also report the second run as a hit and hand back a result from a different build. Environment variables, PDK files and hidden defaults are the usual omissions. Deterministic tools are a prerequisite: if the same inputs can give different outputs, a cache cannot be trusted at all.

## Going deeper

Mokhov, Mitchell and Peyton Jones, "Build Systems à la Carte" (ICFP 2018), on cloud build caches and constructive traces; the Bazel documentation on remote caching.

label: Amdahl's law and parallel speedup
lesson:
# Amdahl's law and parallel speedup

EDA runs are long, and machines have many cores, so every engine author is asked how much faster the tool gets with more threads. Amdahl's law gives the first answer: the part of the run that stays serial, such as reading the database, building data structures or writing results, caps the speedup no matter how many threads are added. Knowing the law tells a tool designer where to spend effort: shrinking the serial fraction often matters more than parallelizing the kernel further.

## Speedup with a serial fraction

Split a single-threaded run of time $T_1$ into a serial fraction $s$ and a parallel fraction $1 - s$. On $p$ threads, ideally only the parallel part shrinks:
$$T_p = T_1\left(s + \frac{1 - s}{p}\right), \qquad S(p) = \frac{T_1}{T_p} = \frac{1}{s + (1 - s)/p}.$$
Example: a global-placement run is 10% serial. On 16 threads, $S = 1/(0.1 + 0.9/16) = 1/0.15625 = 6.4$. Sixteen threads give a speedup of 6.4, and the efficiency $S/p$ is only 40%. The formula is optimistic, since it ignores synchronization, memory bandwidth and load imbalance, so measured speedups are usually lower still.

## The ceiling of one over s

As $p \to \infty$ the parallel term $(1 - s)/p$ goes to zero and
$$\lim_{p \to \infty} S(p) = \frac{1}{s}.$$
Example: a single-threaded detailed-routing run takes 400 s, of which 20 s is serial: $s = 20/400 = 0.05$, so no machine can make it more than 20 times faster. With 32 threads the run reaches $1/(0.05 + 0.95/32) \approx 12.55$, already most of the way to the ceiling, and doubling to 64 threads gives only about 15.42.

The ceiling explains why engine teams attack serial phases: parsing Liberty and LEF/DEF in parallel, building the timing graph concurrently, overlapping file output with computation. Halving the serial fraction doubles the ceiling, which no number of extra cores can do.

## Serial fraction from a target speedup

Turn the law around to set a budget. If a product needs speedup $S$ on $p$ threads, solve $S = 1/(s + (1 - s)/p)$ for $s$:
$$s = \frac{p/S - 1}{p - 1}.$$
Example: a router must run 12 times faster on 16 threads. Then $s = (16/12 - 1)/15 = 0.3333/15 \approx 0.0222$: at most about 2.22% of the single-threaded run may be serial. That number becomes an engineering requirement for every phase outside the parallel kernel.

Amdahl assumes a fixed problem. Gustafson's view, that bigger machines are used for bigger designs, gives a gentler picture when the parallel work grows with the design while the serial setup does not. Both views agree that the serial part has to be measured, not guessed, before parallel work is planned.

## Going deeper

Amdahl, "Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities" (AFIPS 1967); Gustafson, "Reevaluating Amdahl's Law" (CACM 1988); Herlihy and Shavit, "The Art of Multiprocessor Programming", chapter 1.

label: Thread pools and partitioned work
lesson:
# Thread pools and partitioned work

Parallel EDA engines rarely spawn a thread per task. They split the work into pieces (regions for routing, nets for extraction, partitions for placement) and feed them to a fixed pool of worker threads. How the pieces are ordered and assigned decides how close the run gets to the ideal: with uneven pieces, one long task can leave the other workers idle at the end. The makespan, the time until the last worker finishes, is the number to reason about.

## Greedy list scheduling

In list scheduling, tasks wait in a queue and each idle worker takes the next one. Equivalently, each task in order goes to the worker that becomes free first. The makespan is the largest worker load.

Example: tasks of 5, 3, 8, 2, 4 and 6 ms on 2 workers, ties going to the lower-numbered worker. Worker 1 takes 5 and worker 2 takes 3. Worker 2 is free first (at 3), so it takes 8 and is busy until 11. Worker 1 (at 5) takes 2, then at 7 takes 4, ending at 11. Both are at 11; the tie goes to worker 1, which takes 6 and finishes at 17. Makespan: 17 ms, while worker 2 sits idle from 11. Greedy scheduling is never worse than twice the optimum, but the order of the queue matters.

## Longest task first

Sorting the queue from longest to shortest before scheduling, the LPT rule, avoids leaving a long task for the end, when it cannot be balanced against anything. For the same tasks, the order is 8, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2. Worker 1 takes 8, worker 2 takes 6. Worker 2 is free first and takes 5 (ending at 11), worker 1 at 8 takes 4 (12), worker 2 at 11 takes 3 (14), worker 1 at 12 takes 2 (14). Makespan: 14 ms instead of 17.

LPT is guaranteed to be within a factor $4/3 - 1/(3p)$ of optimal. Engines apply the same idea by estimating task cost in advance: routing regions by pin count, nets by fanout. When costs cannot be predicted, smaller pieces and work stealing (an idle worker takes queued work from a busy one) keep the imbalance small at the end.

## Lower bounds on makespan

No schedule on $p$ workers can finish before
$$T^* \ge \max\left(\frac{\sum_i t_i}{p},\ \max_i t_i\right):$$
the total work must be shared among $p$ workers, and the longest task runs on one worker whatever happens. With dependencies between tasks, the longest dependency chain, the critical path, is a further bound.

In the example the total is 28 ms, so 2 workers need at least 14 ms, and the longest task is 8 ms. The bound is 14 ms, which LPT achieves, so LPT is optimal here. Comparing a schedule with this bound tells an engineer whether to fix the scheduler (a large gap) or to split the longest task (when $\max_i t_i$ dominates, as with one giant net or one congested region). A single 8 ms task on 8 workers with 16 ms total work gives a bound of 8 ms, not 2.

## Going deeper

Graham, "Bounds on Multiprocessing Timing Anomalies" (SIAM J. Applied Mathematics, 1969); the Taskflow documentation, used by OpenTimer, for task-graph scheduling with work stealing.
