label: Deterministic parallelism
lesson:
# Deterministic parallelism

A deterministic engine gives bit-identical results for identical inputs, every run. Parallelism threatens this even without bugs: threads finish in different orders, floating-point sums depend on order, and shared random generators hand out numbers by timing. EDA teams insist on determinism because regression testing, bug reproduction, result caching and QoR comparison all assume it. A wirelength that drifts by 0.01% between identical runs hides real 0.01% regressions and makes field bugs impossible to reproduce.

## Floating-point sums depend on order

Floating-point addition rounds after every operation, so it is not associative: $(a + b) + c$ can differ from $a + (b + c)$. In decimal arithmetic rounded to 4 significant digits, $(1000 + 0.4) + 0.4$ rounds to 1000 at each step, while $1000 + (0.4 + 0.4) = 1000 + 0.8 = 1000.8$, which rounds to 1001. Double precision behaves the same way in its last bits.

A parallel reduction (the total wirelength, the density penalty, a gradient sum) combines partial sums in whatever order threads finish. Run twice, it can produce totals that differ in the last digits, with no race and no bug. In an iterative optimizer that difference does not stay small: it flips a comparison, a different move is accepted, and the final placements diverge. So bitwise reproducibility, not just "close enough," is the usual requirement.

## Fixed partitions and ordered merges

The cure is to make every rounding step and every merge independent of timing. Three techniques cover most cases. First, partition statically: split the index range into fixed chunks and compute a partial result per chunk. Second, merge in a fixed order: combine chunk results by chunk index, never as they arrive, and write per-item results into slots keyed by item index rather than appending to a shared list. Third, key randomness to work, not to threads: derive each item's random stream from the run seed and the item index, so the same item sees the same numbers whatever thread runs it.

If the chunking is chosen independently of the thread count, the result is also identical on 4 threads and on 32. A mutex is not a fix: it removes a race, but the order in which threads take the lock still varies, so an order-dependent result still varies.

## Deterministic tie-breaking and thread-count independence

Even single-threaded code hides nondeterminism. Iterating a hash map whose order depends on insertion history or a randomized hash seed, sorting by pointer address, reading uninitialized memory, or picking "the first" of equal-cost candidates from an unordered container all make results vary between runs. The rule is to break every tie with a stable key, such as an instance index or a name, and to sort by persistent ids, never by addresses.

The payoff is practical. A bug found on a 64-core server reproduces on a laptop. A regression that changes QoR on a commit touching only comments points to a determinism bug, not noise. Differential tests can demand identical outputs. Engines such as OpenROAD's tools aim to give the same result for the same inputs and seed, and treat any violation as a defect. The cost is usually a few percent of speed, from static partitioning and ordered merges.

## Going deeper

Goldberg, "What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic" (ACM Computing Surveys, 1991); Demmel and Nguyen, "Fast Reproducible Floating-Point Summation" (ARITH 2013); Bocchino et al., "Parallel Programming Must Be Deterministic by Default" (HotPar 2009).

problems.q:
Which change makes a parallel float sum bitwise reproducible across runs with the same thread count?

A) Statically assign index ranges to threads and combine partial sums in a fixed order

B) Increase the number of threads until the result stabilizes

C) Use dynamic scheduling so every thread stays busy

D) Use an atomic float add into one shared accumulator
problems.a: Statically assign index ranges to threads and combine partial sums in a fixed order
problems.e: A fixed partition and a fixed combine order fix every rounding step. Atomic adds and dynamic scheduling make the order depend on timing.

problems.q:
Why do tiny reduction-order differences matter in a placer more than in a single report?

A) Only the final HPWL report is affected, never the cell positions

B) The engine iterates, so small differences change later decisions and the final placement diverges

C) Placers use integer arithmetic only, so differences cannot occur

D) They do not matter; the final placement is always identical
problems.a: The engine iterates, so small differences change later decisions and the final placement diverges
problems.e: An optimizer's decisions (a move accepted, a cell ordered first) depend on comparisons, and a last-digit change can flip one; the divergence then compounds across iterations.

problems.q:
A placer sums the wirelength gradient over all nets with a parallel reduction. Run twice with the same input and 16 threads, it reports total wirelengths that differ in the 12th digit. What is the cause?

A) A data race corrupted memory in one run

B) Double precision is too short to hold a wirelength

C) The random seed is reset differently on each run

D) Floating-point addition is not associative, and the reduction order differed
problems.a: Floating-point addition is not associative, and the reduction order differed
problems.e: With dynamic scheduling, partial sums are combined in whatever order threads finish. Rounding depends on order, so the last digits move even with no race.

problems.q:
A parallel simulated-annealing step needs random numbers in every worker. Which seeding scheme keeps runs reproducible?

A) Seed each worker from the wall-clock time

B) Derive each work item's stream from the run seed and the item index

C) Share one global generator protected by a lock

D) Seed each worker with its thread ID
problems.a: Derive each work item's stream from the run seed and the item index
problems.e: A shared locked generator hands out numbers in timing-dependent order. A stream keyed by run seed and item index gives every item the same numbers no matter which thread runs it.

problems.q:
A parallel simulated-annealing step needs random numbers in every worker. Which seeding scheme keeps runs reproducible?

A) Seed each worker with its thread ID

B) Share one global generator protected by a lock

C) Seed each worker from the wall-clock time

D) Derive each work item's stream from the run seed and the item index
problems.a: Derive each work item's stream from the run seed and the item index
problems.e: A shared locked generator hands out numbers in timing-dependent order. A stream keyed by run seed and item index gives every item the same numbers no matter which thread runs it.

problems.q:
A team wants results to be identical whether a job runs on 4 threads or 32. Which design achieves that?

A) Give each thread an equal share of the work, sized by the thread count

B) Seed each thread's random generator with its thread ID

C) Partition the work into a fixed number of chunks independent of the thread count and reduce chunks in order

D) Let threads steal work and merge whichever partial result arrives first
problems.a: Partition the work into a fixed number of chunks independent of the thread count and reduce chunks in order
problems.e: If the chunking depends on the thread count, the rounding and the random streams change with it. Fixed chunks with fixed seeds and ordered reduction make the thread count a pure performance knob.

problems.q:
A regression flags a 0.1% wirelength change on a commit that only touched comments. The engine is supposedly deterministic. What should the team suspect first?

A) Wirelength always varies by 0.1% between runs

B) The test design was changed by the commit

C) A hidden source of nondeterminism such as unordered iteration, timing-dependent merging or uninitialized memory

D) The compiler optimized the comments
problems.a: A hidden source of nondeterminism such as unordered iteration, timing-dependent merging or uninitialized memory
problems.e: Deterministic engines should produce bit-identical results from identical inputs. A change without a cause is a determinism bug, and it would hide real regressions.

problems.q:
A tool sorts instances by pointer address to get a stable order for a heuristic. Results differ between runs. Why?

A) Pointers are always sorted in allocation order

B) Pointer comparison is undefined for any two objects

C) Sorting is not stable for equal keys

D) Allocation addresses differ from run to run, so the order changes
problems.a: Allocation addresses differ from run to run, so the order changes
problems.e: Address layout depends on the allocator, address-space randomization and earlier allocations. Use a persistent ID or name as the key.

problems.q:
Why is 'same result regardless of thread count' worth paying a few percent of speed for in a production EDA engine?

A) It removes the need for regression tests

B) It guarantees the result is optimal

C) It makes the engine run faster on many threads

D) Bugs found on a big machine can be reproduced on a laptop, and QoR comparisons are not confounded by run noise
problems.a: Bugs found on a big machine can be reproduced on a laptop, and QoR comparisons are not confounded by run noise
problems.e: Reproducibility makes debugging and differential testing possible. Without it, every QoR delta carries noise from scheduling.

label: Conflict-free parallel batches
lesson:
# Conflict-free parallel batches

Many EDA engines work on a grid of regions: detailed routers route tiles, legalizers repair windows, DRC engines check windows with halos. Neighbouring regions can touch the same wires or cells, so processing them simultaneously would race. Locks per object are slow and nondeterministic. A cleaner scheme colors the regions so that no two neighbours share a color, then processes one color at a time: inside a color, regions are independent and run in parallel with no locks at all.

## Coloring tiles so batches never conflict

Model each tile as a vertex and join two tiles that may conflict; a batch must be an independent set, and a coloring partitions the tiles into batches. For a rectangular grid where tiles conflict when they share an edge or a corner, the coloring by $(r \bmod 2,\ c \bmod 2)$ works: two tiles with the same color differ by at least 2 in row or column, so they never touch. Four colors are also necessary, since any 2 × 2 block contains four mutually adjacent tiles.

Example: a 5 × 7 grid. Rows 0, 2 and 4 are even (3 rows); columns 0, 2, 4 and 6 are even (4 columns). The even-even batch has $3 \times 4 = 12$ tiles. The other batches have $3 \times 3 = 9$, $2 \times 4 = 8$ and $2 \times 3 = 6$, which sum to the 35 tiles. If only edge-sharing tiles conflicted, a checkerboard with two colors would do.

## Rounds with a fixed worker count

Batches run one after another, separated by a barrier, because a tile in a later batch may touch tiles of the current one. Inside a batch of $n_k$ tiles, $p$ workers handle $p$ tiles per round, so the batch takes $\lceil n_k / p \rceil$ rounds, and the whole grid takes
$$R = \sum_{k} \left\lceil \frac{n_k}{p} \right\rceil.$$
For the 5 × 7 grid with $p = 4$: $\lceil 12/4 \rceil + \lceil 9/4 \rceil + \lceil 8/4 \rceil + \lceil 6/4 \rceil = 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 10$ rounds. The ceilings are the cost of the barriers: a batch of 9 tiles leaves three workers idle in its last round. Engines reduce that waste with more tiles than workers, so the last partial round is a small part of each batch, or by letting idle workers begin the next batch's tiles that do not touch unfinished ones.

## Speedup of a batched schedule

If every tile takes the same time $t$, the serial run takes $nt$ for $n$ tiles and the batched run takes $Rt$, so the speedup is $n/R$, at most $p$. For the example, $35/10 = 3.5$ on 4 workers: the partial final rounds cost 12.5%.

The scheme has two further virtues. It is deterministic, because which tiles run together and in what batch order is fixed by the coloring, not by timing, so the results do not depend on thread scheduling. And it needs no locks inside a batch. The trade-off is idle time at barriers and sensitivity to uneven tiles: one congested tile makes its whole batch wait. Real routers therefore size tiles to balance work and process batches with a task pool, but keep the coloring that makes concurrent tiles independent.

## Going deeper

The TritonRoute papers on parallel detailed routing (Kahng, Wang and Xu); Jones and Plassmann, "A Parallel Graph Coloring Heuristic" (SIAM J. Scientific Computing, 1993).

problems.q: A detailed router divides the die into a 5 × 3 grid of tiles (5 rows, 3 columns). Two tiles that share an edge or a corner may touch the same wires, so they must never be routed at the same time. The tiles are colored by (row mod 2, column mod 2), giving four batches; batches run one after another, and inside a batch any tiles may run together. Rows and columns are numbered from 0. How many tiles are in the batch with even row and even column?
problems.e: Even rows: ceil(5/2) = 3. Even columns: ceil(3/2) = 2. The batch holds 3 × 2 = 6 tiles, and no two of them touch, since any two differ by at least two in row or in column.

problems.q: A detailed router divides the die into a 6 × 5 grid of tiles (6 rows, 5 columns). Two tiles that share an edge or a corner may touch the same wires, so they must never be routed at the same time. The tiles are colored by (row mod 2, column mod 2), giving four batches; batches run one after another, and inside a batch any tiles may run together. Rows and columns are numbered from 0. How many tiles are in the batch with even row and even column?
problems.e: Even rows: ceil(6/2) = 3. Even columns: ceil(5/2) = 3. The batch holds 3 × 3 = 9 tiles, and no two of them touch, since any two differ by at least two in row or in column.

problems.q: A detailed router divides the die into a 3 × 5 grid of tiles (3 rows, 5 columns). Two tiles that share an edge or a corner may touch the same wires, so they must never be routed at the same time. The tiles are colored by (row mod 2, column mod 2), giving four batches; batches run one after another, and inside a batch any tiles may run together. Rows and columns are numbered from 0. How many tiles are in the batch with even row and even column?
problems.e: Even rows: ceil(3/2) = 2. Even columns: ceil(5/2) = 3. The batch holds 2 × 3 = 6 tiles, and no two of them touch, since any two differ by at least two in row or in column.

problems.q: A detailed router divides the die into a 3 × 4 grid of tiles (3 rows, 4 columns). Two tiles that share an edge or a corner may touch the same wires, so they must never be routed at the same time. The tiles are colored by (row mod 2, column mod 2), giving four batches; batches run one after another, and inside a batch any tiles may run together. With 6 worker threads, each routing one tile per round, how many rounds does the whole grid take?
problems.e: The four batches hold 4, 4, 2, 2 tiles. Each batch needs ceil(size/6) rounds: 4 tiles → 1 rounds, 4 tiles → 1 rounds, 2 tiles → 1 rounds, 2 tiles → 1 rounds, for 4 rounds in all.

problems.q: A detailed router divides the die into a 7 × 7 grid of tiles (7 rows, 7 columns). Two tiles that share an edge or a corner may touch the same wires, so they must never be routed at the same time. The tiles are colored by (row mod 2, column mod 2), giving four batches; batches run one after another, and inside a batch any tiles may run together. With 3 worker threads, each routing one tile per round, how many rounds does the whole grid take?
problems.e: The four batches hold 16, 12, 12, 9 tiles. Each batch needs ceil(size/3) rounds: 16 tiles → 6 rounds, 12 tiles → 4 rounds, 12 tiles → 4 rounds, 9 tiles → 3 rounds, for 17 rounds in all.

problems.q: A detailed router divides the die into a 5 × 4 grid of tiles (5 rows, 4 columns). Two tiles that share an edge or a corner may touch the same wires, so they must never be routed at the same time. The tiles are colored by (row mod 2, column mod 2), giving four batches; batches run one after another, and inside a batch any tiles may run together. With 3 worker threads, each routing one tile per round, how many rounds does the whole grid take?
problems.e: The four batches hold 6, 6, 4, 4 tiles. Each batch needs ceil(size/3) rounds: 6 tiles → 2 rounds, 6 tiles → 2 rounds, 4 tiles → 2 rounds, 4 tiles → 2 rounds, for 8 rounds in all.

problems.q: A detailed router divides the die into a 5 × 6 grid of tiles (5 rows, 6 columns). Two tiles that share an edge or a corner may touch the same wires, so they must never be routed at the same time. The tiles are colored by (row mod 2, column mod 2), giving four batches; batches run one after another, and inside a batch any tiles may run together. Every tile takes 80 ms. With 2 worker threads, each routing one tile per round, what is the speedup over routing all tiles on one thread? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Serially: 30 tiles × 80 ms = 2400 ms. Batched: 16 rounds (9 tiles → 5 rounds, 9 tiles → 5 rounds, 6 tiles → 3 rounds, 6 tiles → 3 rounds) × 80 ms = 1280 ms. Speedup = 1.88, below 2 because rounds at the end of each batch are only partly full.

problems.q: A detailed router divides the die into a 3 × 5 grid of tiles (3 rows, 5 columns). Two tiles that share an edge or a corner may touch the same wires, so they must never be routed at the same time. The tiles are colored by (row mod 2, column mod 2), giving four batches; batches run one after another, and inside a batch any tiles may run together. Every tile takes 90 ms. With 4 worker threads, each routing one tile per round, what is the speedup over routing all tiles on one thread? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Serially: 15 tiles × 90 ms = 1350 ms. Batched: 5 rounds (6 tiles → 2 rounds, 4 tiles → 1 rounds, 3 tiles → 1 rounds, 2 tiles → 1 rounds) × 90 ms = 450 ms. Speedup = 3, below 4 because rounds at the end of each batch are only partly full.

problems.q: A detailed router divides the die into a 8 × 4 grid of tiles (8 rows, 4 columns). Two tiles that share an edge or a corner may touch the same wires, so they must never be routed at the same time. The tiles are colored by (row mod 2, column mod 2), giving four batches; batches run one after another, and inside a batch any tiles may run together. Every tile takes 20 ms. With 2 worker threads, each routing one tile per round, what is the speedup over routing all tiles on one thread? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Serially: 32 tiles × 20 ms = 640 ms. Batched: 16 rounds (8 tiles → 4 rounds, 8 tiles → 4 rounds, 8 tiles → 4 rounds, 8 tiles → 4 rounds) × 20 ms = 320 ms. Speedup = 2, below 2 because rounds at the end of each batch are only partly full.

label: Distributed runs, containers and the cloud
lesson:
# Distributed runs, containers and the cloud

A single flow run fits on one machine, but EDA work rarely comes as one run: regressions run dozens of designs, sweeps run hundreds of parameter sets, characterization runs thousands of independent simulations. Teams spread that work across clusters and clouds, which raises three problems a tool builder must solve: making every machine run the same software, sizing and paying for the fleet, and moving large design data to where the computation happens without breaking the IP boundary.

## Containers pin the tool environment

A container image packages a flow's user space: tool binaries such as Yosys, OpenROAD and KLayout, the libraries they link, the Python interpreter and its packages. Every host that runs the image sees the same versions, so a flow that passed in CI behaves the same on a laptop and on a cluster node. Containers share the host's Linux kernel; isolation comes from kernel namespaces, and resource limits from cgroups, which can cap a job's memory and CPU so that one runaway router does not take down the other jobs on the node.

Reproducibility depends on naming the image exactly. A mutable tag such as latest can be moved to a new build; pinning an image by its content digest names one immutable image. The PDK and design data are usually mounted into the container rather than baked in, which keeps images small and keeps proprietary data out of shared registries.

## Sizing a parameter sweep

For $J$ independent jobs of $t$ hours each on $M$ machines that run one job at a time, the jobs run in $\lceil J/M \rceil$ waves, so the wall-clock time is $\lceil J/M \rceil\, t$. Cost depends on billing. If machines are reserved for the whole sweep, you pay for $M \lceil J/M \rceil t$ machine-hours, idle ones in the last wave included. If an autoscaling pool bills only while a job runs, you pay for $J t$ machine-hours whatever $M$ is: the pool size changes the wall time, not the cost.

Example: 50 runs of 2 h on 8 machines take $\lceil 50/8 \rceil = 7$ waves, 14 h. Reserved at 1.5 credits per machine-hour, the cost is $8 \times 14 \times 1.5 = 168$ credits; billed per job, it is $50 \times 2 \times 1.5 = 150$ credits. Adding machines to 50 would cut the wall time to 2 h at the same per-job cost.

## Scheduling, storage and data locality

Independent jobs scale out almost perfectly; one tightly coupled run that shares a large in-memory database does not, because splitting it across machines turns memory accesses into network messages. So EDA distribution is mostly about many independent jobs, orchestrated as a graph of steps by a scheduler or workflow engine. Two engineering points dominate. Storage: hundreds of jobs reading a 30 GB database each at the same moment saturate a shared file system, so inputs are staged or cached near the compute. Restartability: if each step writes its outputs to durable storage keyed by its inputs, a failed sweep resumes from where it stopped, and cheap preemptible machines become usable for short jobs.

Cloud use also raises an architectural question that is not about price: foundry agreements and IP policy constrain where design and PDK data may live and who may access it, so tenancy, encryption and data residency are part of the design.

## Going deeper

The Linux kernel documentation on cgroups and namespaces; the OpenROAD-flow-scripts documentation on running the flow in Docker; Dean and Barroso, "The Tail at Scale" (CACM 2013), on large-fleet job behaviour.

problems.q:
A container image tag such as latest is used in a regression flow. Why is that risky?

A) Containers ignore tags at run time

B) A tag forces the container to run as root

C) Tags slow down image pulls

D) The tag can point to a different image later, so the flow is not reproducible
problems.a: The tag can point to a different image later, so the flow is not reproducible
problems.e: A mutable tag can be moved to a new build. Pinning an image by its content digest names exactly one image.

problems.q:
A flow that ran cleanly last month now fails at synthesis on a new machine. The team ships the flow as a container image built from a fixed recipe. What does the image guarantee?

A) That the design's QoR improves

B) The same CPU microarchitecture on every host

C) The same tool binaries, libraries and versions on every host that runs it

D) That no license server is needed
problems.a: The same tool binaries, libraries and versions on every host that runs it
problems.e: A container packages the user-space environment, so tool and library versions are pinned. The kernel and hardware still come from the host.

problems.q:
A memory-hungry routing job is run inside a container with a cgroup memory limit of 64 GB and exceeds it. What happens?

A) The container automatically grows its limit

B) Other containers on the host are killed first

C) The kernel kills the process in that cgroup when it cannot reclaim memory

D) The job swaps to the network file system
problems.a: The kernel kills the process in that cgroup when it cannot reclaim memory
problems.e: cgroups enforce resource limits per group. Exceeding the memory limit triggers the out-of-memory killer for that group, which protects the other jobs on the host.

problems.q:
A sweep of 40 flow runs, 2 h each, runs on an autoscaling pool of up to 27 machines; a machine is billed only while it runs a job, at 1.75 credits per machine-hour. What does the sweep cost?

A) 140 credits

B) 280 credits

C) 189 credits

D) 7 credits
problems.a: 140 credits
problems.e: Billing follows the work, not the wall time: 40 jobs × 2 h × 1.75 = 140 credits. The pool size changes the 4 h wall time, not the cost.

problems.q:
A design-space exploration launches 38 independent flow runs, one per parameter set, on 15 identical cloud machines that each run one job at a time. Every run takes 0.5 h. What is the wall-clock time of the sweep?

A) 1.5 h

B) 1 h

C) 19 h

D) 2 h

E) 1.3 h
problems.e: The jobs run in ceil(38/15) = 3 waves of 0.5 h, so the sweep takes 1.5 h.

problems.q:
A sweep of 23 flow runs, 1.5 h each, runs on an autoscaling pool of up to 6 machines; a machine is billed only while it runs a job, at 1.5 credits per machine-hour. What does the sweep cost?

A) 54 credits

B) 103.5 credits

C) 9 credits

D) 51.75 credits
problems.a: 51.75 credits
problems.e: Billing follows the work, not the wall time: 23 jobs × 1.5 h × 1.5 = 51.75 credits. The pool size changes the 6 h wall time, not the cost.

problems.q:
Which job type benefits least from being split across many machines?

A) Characterizing each standard cell of a library separately

B) A sweep of 200 independent flow runs with different parameters

C) One tightly coupled detailed-routing run that shares one in-memory database

D) Running each regression design as its own job
problems.a: One tightly coupled detailed-routing run that shares one in-memory database
problems.e: Independent jobs scale out trivially. A single run that needs fast access to one shared database pays heavy communication costs when distributed.

problems.q:
A workflow orchestrator runs a flow as a graph of steps, each in its own container. A step fails halfway through a 100-step sweep. What property lets the sweep resume without redoing finished steps?

A) Every step runs in the same container

B) Steps share global variables in memory

C) Each step writes its outputs to durable storage keyed by its inputs

D) The orchestrator restarts the sweep from the beginning
problems.a: Each step writes its outputs to durable storage keyed by its inputs
problems.e: If finished outputs are recorded against their inputs, the orchestrator can skip completed steps and rerun only what failed or depends on it.

problems.q:
A cluster scheduler places 500 flow jobs. Each reads a 30 GB design database from shared storage. What is the likely bottleneck?

A) The number of Linux users on the cluster

B) CPU cycles spent parsing the scheduler's job file

C) The container image size on each host

D) Shared storage bandwidth while all jobs load their inputs
problems.a: Shared storage bandwidth while all jobs load their inputs
problems.e: Hundreds of jobs reading large inputs at once saturate the file system. Staging data locally or caching inputs near the compute relieves it.

label: License management and tool economics
prereqs: Distributed runs, containers and the cloud
lesson:
# License management and tool economics

Commercial EDA tools are licensed, usually as a pool of floating licenses served by a license server: a job checks out a license when it starts a licensed feature and checks it back in when done. Licenses, not machines, are often the scarce resource, since a site may have thousands of cores but a few dozen licenses of a signoff tool. Planning around licenses is ordinary scheduling arithmetic, and tool and flow builders influence it directly by deciding when a license is held.

## Licenses cap concurrency

If every job needs one license for its whole run and machines are plentiful, at most $L$ jobs run at once. $J$ jobs of $t$ hours then run in $\lceil J/L \rceil$ waves, and the batch takes $\lceil J/L \rceil\, t$ hours.

Example: 23 signoff timing runs of 3 h each with 5 licenses run in $\lceil 23/5 \rceil = 5$ waves: 15 h. Adding machines does nothing; adding a sixth license gives $\lceil 23/6 \rceil = 4$ waves, 12 h, and an eighth gives 3 waves, 9 h. This is why license counts are negotiated against schedules: a tape-out crunch that needs many signoff runs in parallel is a license question first. Open-source tools remove this constraint entirely, one of their practical attractions for regressions and sweeps, where thousands of runs would otherwise queue for licenses.

## License utilization

Over a batch, the licenses offer $L \times T_{wall}$ license-hours, and the jobs use $J t$. Utilization is
$$U = \frac{J t}{L\, \lceil J/L \rceil\, t} = \frac{J}{L \lceil J/L \rceil}.$$
In the example, $U = 23/(5 \times 5) = 92\%$: the last wave has only 3 jobs, so 2 licenses sit idle for 3 h. With 20 jobs, utilization would be 100%; with 21, a fifth wave holds a single job and $U = 21/25 = 84\%$.

Licenses are expensive, so sites measure utilization from license-server logs and fill idle capacity with lower-priority jobs. Queueing systems that are aware of licenses hold a job until its license is free, instead of starting it and letting it wait while it occupies a machine.

## Check in licenses early

A job holds a license for as long as it keeps it checked out, which is not necessarily its whole run. Suppose each job has a licensed phase of $b$ hours (the timing analysis itself) and then $c$ hours of unlicensed work (parsing reports, plotting, archiving). Holding the license until the end makes each job occupy it for $b + c$ hours: the batch takes $\lceil J/L \rceil (b + c)$. Checking in after the licensed phase lets the next job start: licensed phases run back to back in $\lceil J/L \rceil$ waves of $b$, and only the last wave's post-processing adds $c$, for $\lceil J/L \rceil\, b + c$.

Example: 12 jobs, 4 licenses, $b = 2$ h, $c = 1$ h. Holding: $3 \times 3 = 9$ h. Checking in: $3 \times 2 + 1 = 7$ h, saving 2 h with the same licenses. Flow builders apply the same idea by splitting jobs so that licensed steps do only licensed work.

## Going deeper

Vendor documentation for floating license servers (for example the FlexNet Publisher administration guide); Kahng et al., "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 1, on design cost and tools.

problems.q: A team must run 7 signoff timing jobs, each holding one tool license for its whole 1 h run. Machines are plentiful, but only 3 licenses exist. What is the wall-clock time to finish all jobs, in hours?
problems.e: At most 3 jobs run at once, so the jobs run in ceil(7/3) = 3 waves of 1 h: 3 h.

problems.q: A team must run 16 signoff timing jobs, each holding one tool license for its whole 3 h run. Machines are plentiful, but only 5 licenses exist. What is the wall-clock time to finish all jobs, in hours?
problems.e: At most 5 jobs run at once, so the jobs run in ceil(16/5) = 4 waves of 3 h: 12 h.

problems.q: A team must run 21 signoff timing jobs, each holding one tool license for its whole 6 h run. Machines are plentiful, but only 6 licenses exist. What is the wall-clock time to finish all jobs, in hours?
problems.e: At most 6 jobs run at once, so the jobs run in ceil(21/6) = 4 waves of 6 h: 24 h.

problems.q: 7 jobs of 2 h each share 3 licenses, each job holding one license for its whole run, and run in back-to-back waves. Over the wall-clock time of the batch, what percentage of the available license-hours is in use? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: The batch takes 3 waves × 2 h = 6 h, offering 3 × 6 = 18 license-hours. Jobs use 7 × 2 = 14, so utilization is 77.78%. The last wave is only partly full.

problems.q: 11 jobs of 6 h each share 7 licenses, each job holding one license for its whole run, and run in back-to-back waves. Over the wall-clock time of the batch, what percentage of the available license-hours is in use? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: The batch takes 2 waves × 6 h = 12 h, offering 7 × 12 = 84 license-hours. Jobs use 11 × 6 = 66, so utilization is 78.57%. The last wave is only partly full.

problems.q: 11 jobs of 3 h each share 3 licenses, each job holding one license for its whole run, and run in back-to-back waves. Over the wall-clock time of the batch, what percentage of the available license-hours is in use? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: The batch takes 4 waves × 3 h = 12 h, offering 3 × 12 = 36 license-hours. Jobs use 11 × 3 = 33, so utilization is 91.67%. The last wave is only partly full.

problems.q: Each of 20 jobs has a 3 h phase that needs the tool license, followed by a 1 h post-processing phase (report parsing and plotting) that does not. There are 5 licenses and plenty of machines. How many hours of wall-clock time are saved if each job checks its license back in when the licensed phase ends, instead of holding it until the job finishes?
problems.e: Holding: 4 waves × (3 + 1) h = 16 h. Checking in: the licensed phases run back to back in 4 waves of 3 h, and the last wave's post-processing adds 1 h, so 13 h. Saved: 3 h.

problems.q: Each of 9 jobs has a 2 h phase that needs the tool license, followed by a 4 h post-processing phase (report parsing and plotting) that does not. There are 2 licenses and plenty of machines. How many hours of wall-clock time are saved if each job checks its license back in when the licensed phase ends, instead of holding it until the job finishes?
problems.e: Holding: 5 waves × (2 + 4) h = 30 h. Checking in: the licensed phases run back to back in 5 waves of 2 h, and the last wave's post-processing adds 4 h, so 14 h. Saved: 16 h.

problems.q: Each of 18 jobs has a 1 h phase that needs the tool license, followed by a 4 h post-processing phase (report parsing and plotting) that does not. There are 8 licenses and plenty of machines. How many hours of wall-clock time are saved if each job checks its license back in when the licensed phase ends, instead of holding it until the job finishes?
problems.e: Holding: 3 waves × (1 + 4) h = 15 h. Checking in: the licensed phases run back to back in 3 waves of 1 h, and the last wave's post-processing adds 4 h, so 7 h. Saved: 8 h.

label: Regression testing and QoR tracking
lesson:
# Regression testing and QoR tracking

An EDA engine is never finished: every heuristic tweak, refactor or compiler upgrade can change results. Regression testing runs a fixed suite of designs through the tool on every change and compares quality of results (QoR), such as wirelength, worst slack, area, power and run time, against a stored baseline. The comparison must summarize many designs of very different sizes into one honest number, and the standard summary is the geometric mean of per-design ratios.

## Geometric mean of QoR ratios

For each design $i$, form the ratio $r_i = \text{new}_i / \text{old}_i$ of the candidate's metric to the baseline's. A ratio is scale free: a 1% change on a tiny design and on a huge one count equally, which raw differences would not. Summarize $n$ ratios by their geometric mean,
$$G = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} r_i\right)^{1/n} = \exp\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \ln r_i\right).$$
Example: routed wirelength on three designs goes 1000 → 900, 500 → 550 and 2000 → 2000. The ratios are 0.9, 1.1 and 1.0. Their product is 0.99, so $G = 0.99^{1/3} \approx 0.997$. Computing through logarithms avoids overflow and underflow when the suite has hundreds of designs.

## Reporting a percent change

A geometric-mean ratio is reported as a signed percentage, $(G - 1) \times 100$. For the example, $(0.9967 - 1) \times 100 \approx -0.33\%$: for a lower-is-better metric, a 0.33% improvement on average. Regression dashboards show this per metric and per commit, so a slow drift becomes visible long before any single design looks broken.

A summary must not hide outliers. A suite whose geometric mean improves by 1% while one design gets 15% worse has a real problem, so dashboards also show the per-design ratios and flag any design beyond a tolerance. Run time needs its own baseline machine and load, since it varies with the host, and metrics with mixed directions (lower is better for area, higher for slack margin) should be put on a common orientation before they are combined. Worst slack, which can be zero or negative, is better tracked as a difference than as a ratio.

## Why the geometric mean is symmetric

Compare the candidate with the baseline, or the baseline with the candidate: the conclusion should be the same. The geometric mean has exactly this property, because the geometric mean of the reciprocals is the reciprocal of the geometric mean:
$$\left(\prod_i \frac{1}{r_i}\right)^{1/n} = \frac{1}{G}.$$
For the example, baseline over candidate gives $1/0.9967 \approx 1.003$, the same 0.33% read from the other side.

The arithmetic mean fails this test. Take two designs, one twice as large and one half as large: ratios 2 and 0.5. Their arithmetic mean is 1.25, which says the candidate is 25% worse, and the arithmetic mean of the reciprocals, 0.5 and 2, is also 1.25, which says the baseline is 25% worse. Both cannot be true. The geometric mean gives 1 both ways, the correct reading of a gain and a loss that cancel in ratio terms.

## Going deeper

Fleming and Wallace, "How Not to Lie with Statistics: The Correct Way to Summarize Benchmark Results" (CACM 1986); the OpenROAD-flow-scripts documentation on its metrics and regression checks.

label: Seed noise and QoR significance
lesson:
# Seed noise and QoR significance

Placers and routers use randomness: initial positions, move orders, tie-breaking seeds. Change the seed and wirelength moves by a fraction of a percent with no change to the code. A regression that reports a 0.3% improvement is meaningless unless that number is compared with the seed-to-seed noise. Running several seeds before and after a change, and testing the paired differences, separates real improvements from luck. It is ordinary statistics, applied to the most common question in engine development.

## Paired differences across seeds

Run the old and the new build with the same seeds $1, \ldots, n$ and record the metric for each. Pairing removes the variation that the seed causes in both builds alike: a seed that happens to give a good placement gives a good one before and after. Analyze the per-seed differences $d_i = \text{after}_i - \text{before}_i$.

Example: routed wirelength in mm for four seeds, before → after: 500 → 497, 512 → 510, 488 → 487 and 505 → 498. The differences are $-3, -2, -1, -7$, and their mean is $\bar d = -13/4 = -3.25$ mm. A negative mean suggests that the change shortens wirelength. Whether -3.25 is real depends on how much the differences scatter. Pairing is legitimate only if the seed has the same meaning in both builds; if the change consumes random numbers in a different order, the pairing weakens and more seeds are needed.

## Seed-to-seed spread

The sample standard deviation of the differences measures their scatter:
$$s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n - 1}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (d_i - \bar d)^2}.$$
Dividing by $n - 1$ rather than $n$ makes $s^2$ an unbiased estimate of the variance, which matters for the handful of seeds a regression can afford.

For the example, deviations from -3.25 are $0.25, 1.25, 2.25, -3.75$, with squares $0.0625, 1.5625, 5.0625, 14.0625$ summing to 20.75. Then $s = \sqrt{20.75/3} \approx 2.63$ mm. A spread of 2.63 mm against a mean of 3.25 mm says that individual seeds disagree considerably about the size of the effect. Knowing the typical spread of each metric on each design also sets sensible tolerances for the nightly regression: a band narrower than the seed noise would fail on noise alone.

## The paired t statistic

The paired t statistic divides the mean difference by its standard error:
$$t = \frac{\bar d}{s / \sqrt{n}}.$$
For the example, $t = -3.25 / (2.63/\sqrt 4) = -3.25 / 1.315 \approx -2.47$. Under the null hypothesis of no effect, $t$ follows a t distribution with $n - 1 = 3$ degrees of freedom, whose two-sided 5% critical value is about 3.18. Since $|t| = 2.47 < 3.18$, four seeds are not enough to call the improvement real at that level, though they hint at one.

More seeds shrink the standard error as $1/\sqrt n$, so quadrupling the seeds halves it. The practical lesson for tool builders: report QoR changes with their uncertainty, choose the number of seeds from the noise of each metric, and remember that testing many metrics on many designs at once produces false alarms unless the threshold accounts for it.

## Going deeper

Montgomery, "Design and Analysis of Experiments", chapter 2 on paired comparisons; Kahng and Mantik, "On Mismatches between Incremental Optimizers and Instance Perturbations in Physical Design Tools" (ICCAD 2000), on noise in placement results.

label: Build systems and incremental compilation
lesson:
# Build systems and incremental compilation

A modern EDA tool is millions of lines of C++ across thousands of files, and an engineer, or an agent in a harness loop, rebuilds it many times a day. A build system turns a source edit into the smallest set of recompilations and links that produce a correct binary. It does so with the same machinery as incremental computation: a dependency graph from sources and headers to object files to libraries, and invalidation that follows the graph. Header structure, more than compiler speed, decides how long an edit takes to test.

## Header changes recompile their dependents

In C++, each source file plus everything it includes is a translation unit, compiled to one object file. A translation unit depends on every header it includes directly or through other headers. Editing a header therefore invalidates every translation unit that reaches it in the include graph: a reverse reachability question.

Example: geom.h is included by db.h; net.h includes db.h; place.cpp includes net.h, route.cpp includes db.h, sta.cpp includes timer.h, and gui.cpp includes geom.h. An edit to geom.h recompiles place.cpp (through net.h and db.h), route.cpp (through db.h) and gui.cpp (directly): 3 translation units. An edit to timer.h recompiles only sta.cpp. Build tools such as Make with compiler-generated dependency files, or Ninja under CMake, record these edges after each compile, so the next build knows exactly which objects are stale.

## Parallel compile and the link step

Stale translation units are independent, so the build compiles them in parallel, up to $p$ jobs at once, and then links. If $k$ units each take $c$ seconds, the compile phase needs $\lceil k/p \rceil$ waves and the build takes $\lceil k/p \rceil\, c + L$, with $L$ the link time.

Example: an edit to a low-level header dirties 7 units of 20 s each, the build runs 4 jobs and the link takes 12 s: $\lceil 7/4 \rceil \times 20 + 12 = 52$ s. A one-line change in a .cpp file costs one compile and the link, 32 s. For small edits the link dominates, which is why large tools split into shared libraries or use fast linkers, and why compiler caches such as ccache, which return a stored object when the preprocessed input is unchanged, pay off when switching branches.

## Finding the most expensive header

The cost of touching a header is the number of translation units that reach it, so headers near the bottom of the include graph (core types, geometry, logging) are the expensive ones. A useful audit computes, for every header, its count of dependent translation units and looks at the largest.

In the example, geom.h has 3 dependents, db.h has 2, net.h and timer.h have 1 each: geom.h is the hot spot. Remedies are structural. Forward declarations let a header mention a type without including its definition. Splitting a large header separates rarely changing interfaces from frequently changing details. Keeping implementation out of headers, rather than in inline functions and templates, stops internal edits from rippling outward. These are the same narrow-interface rules that make an engine easy to extend: a plug-in that compiles against a small, stable header rebuilds in seconds when only the plug-in changes.

## Going deeper

Lakos, "Large-Scale C++ Software Design" (1996) and "Large-Scale C++, Volume I" (2019); the Ninja and CMake documentation; Mokhov, Mitchell and Peyton Jones, "Build Systems à la Carte" (ICFP 2018).

label: Continuous integration for EDA tools
lesson:
# Continuous integration for EDA tools

Continuous integration builds the tool and runs its tests on every proposed change, before it merges. For EDA tools the tests are expensive: a regression design takes minutes to hours, and the meaningful checks are QoR comparisons against baselines, not just pass or fail. A CI pipeline therefore has to be engineered like a parallel job: sharded across runners to meet a time budget, tiered so cheap checks run first, and robust against flaky tests that fail without a real bug.

## Wall time of a sharded test stage

A test stage with $N$ designs of $t$ minutes each, spread over $R$ runners, gives each runner at most $\lceil N/R \rceil$ designs. Each runner usually first builds or downloads the tool, a fixed setup time $S$. The stage wall time is
$$W = S + \left\lceil \frac{N}{R} \right\rceil t.$$
Example: 30 designs of 4 min on 6 runners with 8 min of setup: $8 + 5 \times 4 = 28$ min. On 12 runners: $8 + 3 \times 4 = 20$ min. Setup is paid on every runner in parallel, so it bounds the wall time from below and becomes the main cost as runners are added. Building the tool once and sharing the binary as a CI artifact turns per-runner setup into a download, and real suites balance shards by measured design run times rather than by count.

## Runners needed to meet a budget

Given a budget $B$ minutes, the stage fits if $S + \lceil N/R \rceil t \le B$, that is, if each runner gets at most $K = \lfloor (B - S)/t \rfloor$ designs. The fewest runners is then $R = \lceil N/K \rceil$.

Example: a pull-request check must finish in 30 min, with 45 designs of 5 min and 10 min of setup. $K = \lfloor 20/5 \rfloor = 4$ designs per runner, so $R = \lceil 45/4 \rceil = 12$ runners, which gives $10 + 4 \times 5 = 30$ min. Eleven runners would need 5 designs on some runner, 35 min. When no affordable runner count fits, the suite is tiered: a small, fast set of designs gates every pull request, and the full suite with QoR comparison runs nightly against the main branch.

## Flaky tests and retries

A flaky test fails sometimes on correct code: a timeout on a loaded runner, a race in the test harness, a nondeterministic engine. If $f$ flaky tests each fail independently with probability $q$, a correct commit passes all of them with probability $(1 - q)^f$. With $f = 5$ and $q = 0.05$, that is $0.95^5 \approx 77.38\%$: almost one correct commit in four is blocked.

Rerunning a failed flaky test once, and accepting a pass, cuts its failure probability to $q^2 = 0.0025$, so all five pass with probability $(1 - 0.0025)^5 \approx 98.76\%$. Retries are a stopgap with a cost: they hide nondeterminism that may be a real engine bug, and a test that passes on retry should be logged and fixed. For EDA engines, a QoR test that is flaky usually means the engine is not deterministic, which is exactly the property CI exists to protect.

## Going deeper

Humble and Farley, "Continuous Delivery" (2010); Luo et al., "An Empirical Analysis of Flaky Tests" (FSE 2014); the OpenROAD and OpenROAD-flow-scripts repositories' CI configuration as working examples.

problems.q: A CI job for an open-source placer runs 30 regression designs, each taking 3 min, split evenly across 2 runners. Each runner first spends 12 min building the tool. problems.e: Each runner builds for 12 min, then runs at most ceil(30/2) = 15 designs of 3 min: 12 + 45 = 57 min.

label: Version control and bisecting regressions
lesson:
# Version control and bisecting regressions

Version control gives every state of the tool a name, a commit, and lets anyone rebuild any of them. That turns a regression into a search problem: if last week's build was good and today's is bad, the culprit is one of the commits in between. Bisection finds it by binary search over history. For EDA tools, where each test means building the tool and running a design for many minutes, the logarithmic cost of bisection is the difference between an hour and a week.

## Halving the suspect range

Suppose $n$ commits separate a known good build from a known bad one, so the first bad commit is one of $n$ suspects, the bad endpoint included. Bisection tests the middle suspect: if it is bad, the culprit is at or before it; if good, after it. Each test halves the range, so identifying the culprit takes at most
$$\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$$
tests. Example: 200 commits between a good and a bad nightly need $\lceil \log_2 200 \rceil = 8$ tests, since $2^7 = 128 < 200 \le 256 = 2^8$.

Git automates the bookkeeping: git bisect checks out the midpoint, the engineer or a script marks it good or bad, and it proposes the next commit. A script that builds the tool, runs the design and compares a QoR threshold can drive the whole search unattended. The test must be deterministic, or a noisy QoR measure will steer bisection the wrong way.

## Time to find the culprit

Each bisection step costs a build and a test run, so the worst-case time is
$$T = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil\,(t_{build} + t_{test}).$$
Example: 200 suspects, a 15 min build and a 40 min design run: $8 \times 55 = 440$ min, just over 7 hours, unattended. Reducing either term pays off 8 times: a compiler cache that cuts the build to 5 min saves 80 min, and a smaller design that still shows the regression saves far more.

Two practical complications. Some commits do not build, or fail for an unrelated reason; bisection can skip them, at the cost of possibly ending with a small range rather than one commit. And a regression may need two commits to interact, which a single bisection cannot isolate. Keeping commits small and individually buildable is what makes history searchable.

## Bisection against a linear scan

A linear scan tests suspects one by one, oldest first. If the first $n - 1$ all pass, the last one is the culprit without testing it, so the worst case is $n - 1$ tests, against $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ for bisection.

For 200 suspects, that is 199 tests against 8: 191 extra build-and-run cycles, or several days at 55 min each. The gap grows quickly, since doubling the range adds only one bisection step. The comparison also explains why per-commit CI matters even though bisection is efficient: a regression caught on the commit that introduced it needs no search at all, while a regression found weeks later, across thousands of commits by many authors, still costs a dozen expensive steps and a confusing history. Nightly QoR tracking sits in between: it bounds the search to one day's commits, typically a few dozen.

## Going deeper

Chacon and Straub, "Pro Git" (2nd ed.), section on git bisect; Zeller, "Why Programs Fail" (2nd ed., 2009), chapter on delta debugging.

label: C++ and Rust in EDA
lesson:
# C++ and Rust in EDA

Almost every production EDA engine, commercial or open source, has a C++ core: OpenROAD, OpenSTA, Yosys, KLayout, Verilator and Xyce among them. The choice is not fashion. Engines touch hundreds of millions of objects in tight loops and need control of memory layout and native speed. C++ also brings use-after-free bugs, data races and a fragile binary interface. Rust is increasingly used for new components because it removes whole classes of these bugs at compile time, and real tools increasingly mix the two, which makes the boundary between languages a design problem.

## Why EDA cores are written in C++

Three properties keep C++ at the core. Performance: compiled native code, templates that the compiler instantiates and inlines per type, and no interpreter or garbage collector between the algorithm and memory. Layout control: the engineer decides whether instances live in arrays of structures or structures of arrays, uses 32-bit ids instead of 64-bit pointers, and pools allocations, which decides cache behaviour on large designs. Ecosystem: decades of EDA code, libraries and expertise.

The costs are equally concrete. Manual memory management produces dangling pointers, for example a stale pointer to an instance that an optimizer deleted. The C++ ABI, including name mangling, class layout and standard-library internals, differs between compilers and versions, so a plug-in built with one toolchain can crash when it receives a std::string from another. Long compile times come from heavy headers and templates. Large EDA code bases control these risks with handle-based object access, sanitizers in CI and narrow C-style plug-in boundaries.

## What Rust's ownership buys

Rust's ownership rules say that every value has one owner, and that at any moment there is either any number of shared references to it or exactly one mutable reference. The compiler enforces this, so safe Rust code cannot use freed memory and cannot have data races: a router that shares a read-only grid among threads and gives each thread exclusive mutable access to its own region compiles, while one in which two threads could write the same cell does not.

Rust does not make an engine deterministic: floating-point reductions in timing-dependent order still vary, which remains the programmer's job. And single ownership fits cyclic pointer graphs badly; a netlist where nets point to pins and pins point back to nets is awkward with references. Rust EDA code therefore usually stores objects in arenas or vectors and refers to them by integer index, the same id-based pattern good C++ databases use, which also happens to be cache friendly.

## Crossing language boundaries

Real tools mix languages: a C++ core, Tcl and Python for scripting, and increasingly Rust components. Every boundary needs a contract. OpenROAD exposes its C++ engines to Tcl and Python through wrappers generated by SWIG, glue code that converts arguments and wraps native objects in script handles. A script that keeps a handle to an instance the engine has since deleted can crash or read garbage unless the binding checks validity, so ownership across the boundary must be designed, for instance by passing ids that are checked on use.

Between Rust and C++, the robust interface is the C ABI: plain structs, explicit create and destroy functions, and no language-specific types such as std::vector or Vec crossing the line. Memory-safety guarantees stop at that boundary; the unsafe wrapper code must uphold lifetimes and aliasing by hand. A rule of thumb for new components: hot per-object loops in C++ or Rust, orchestration and report post-processing in Python.

## Going deeper

Stroustrup, "A Tour of C++" (3rd ed., 2022); Klabnik and Nichols, "The Rust Programming Language" (the Rust book), chapters on ownership and fearless concurrency; the SWIG documentation and OpenROAD's developer guide on its Tcl and Python bindings.

problems.q:
A C++ timer library is distributed as a compiled shared library, and a plug-in built with a different compiler version crashes when it receives a std::string. What is the cause?

A) std::string cannot cross a function call

B) Shared libraries cannot export functions

C) The plug-in forgot to include the header

D) The C++ ABI, including standard-library layouts, is not stable across compilers and versions
problems.a: The C++ ABI, including standard-library layouts, is not stable across compilers and versions
problems.e: Name mangling, class layout and standard-library internals may differ between toolchains. Stable plug-in boundaries use C ABI functions and plain data.

problems.q:
A C++ timer library is distributed as a compiled shared library, and a plug-in built with a different compiler version crashes when it receives a std::string. What is the cause?

A) The plug-in forgot to include the header

B) The C++ ABI, including standard-library layouts, is not stable across compilers and versions

C) Shared libraries cannot export functions

D) std::string cannot cross a function call
problems.a: The C++ ABI, including standard-library layouts, is not stable across compilers and versions
problems.e: Name mangling, class layout and standard-library internals may differ between toolchains. Stable plug-in boundaries use C ABI functions and plain data.

problems.q:
Why are the hot kernels of most production EDA engines (timers, routers, placers) written in C++ rather than in Python?

A) Python cannot express graph algorithms

B) Python cannot read text files as large as Liberty

C) They need predictable native speed, control of memory layout and no interpreter overhead per object

D) C++ programs need no testing
problems.a: They need predictable native speed, control of memory layout and no interpreter overhead per object
problems.e: Engines touch hundreds of millions of objects in tight loops. Native code with controlled layout is orders of magnitude faster than interpreted per-object work.

problems.q:
A Rust router shares a read-only routing grid among threads and gives each thread exclusive mutable access to its own region. What does the compiler check?

A) That no data is mutated while another thread can read or write it

B) That the routing is DRC-clean

C) That the program uses no heap memory

D) That the threads finish in a fixed order
problems.a: That no data is mutated while another thread can read or write it
problems.e: Ownership and borrowing rules enforce shared-xor-mutable access at compile time, which rules out data races in safe code. They do not guarantee a deterministic order.

problems.q:
Which guarantee does safe Rust NOT give a parallel EDA engine?

A) That floating-point reductions produce the same bits on every run

B) That a freed object cannot be accessed

C) That no two threads mutate the same data at once

D) That references never outlive what they point to
problems.a: That floating-point reductions produce the same bits on every run
problems.e: Memory safety and race freedom are enforced, but reduction order and other sources of nondeterminism are still the programmer's responsibility.

problems.q:
A netlist graph has nets pointing to pins and pins pointing back to nets. Why is this awkward in safe Rust, and what do Rust EDA codes often do?

A) Rust copies the whole graph on every access

B) Cyclic references conflict with single ownership, so they store objects in arenas and refer to them by index

C) They use reference counting for every pin, which is free

D) Rust forbids graphs, so they use a C++ library instead
problems.a: Cyclic references conflict with single ownership, so they store objects in arenas and refer to them by index
problems.e: Single ownership makes cyclic pointer graphs hard. Arena storage with integer ids, the same pattern many C++ databases use, keeps the graph simple and cache friendly.

problems.q:
A Rust plug-in must be called from a C++ engine. What interface is the most robust to put between them?

A) C++ classes with virtual functions shared directly

B) Rust generic functions exported by name

C) A C ABI with plain structs and explicit create and destroy functions

D) Passing std::vector and Vec values directly
problems.a: A C ABI with plain structs and explicit create and destroy functions
problems.e: Both languages speak the C ABI. Plain data and explicit ownership functions avoid relying on either language's unstable layouts.

problems.q:
When is it reasonable to write a new EDA tool component in Python rather than C++ or Rust?

A) When it implements the inner loop of a detailed router

B) Never, because Python cannot call native code

C) When it orchestrates engines or post-processes reports, not when it runs a hot per-object loop

D) When it must process a billion polygons per second
problems.a: When it orchestrates engines or post-processes reports, not when it runs a hot per-object loop
problems.e: Flow control, reporting and glue are cheap relative to the engines they call; inner loops over design objects belong in native code.

problems.q:
A Python script holds a handle to a database instance, then a C++ engine deletes that instance. What can happen when the script uses the handle?

A) The engine automatically re-creates the instance

B) Python's garbage collector restores the instance

C) The handle may dangle and crash or read garbage unless the binding checks validity

D) Nothing, because Python owns all database objects
problems.a: The handle may dangle and crash or read garbage unless the binding checks validity
problems.e: The binding wraps a native pointer that Python cannot track. Ownership across the boundary has to be designed, for example with ids checked on access.

label: The SKY130 open PDK
prereqs: What a process design kit contains
lesson:
# The SKY130 open PDK

SKY130 is the SkyWater 130 nm process, released as an open process design kit with Google's backing. It was the first open PDK that a full digital flow could target end to end, so it is where most open-source EDA tools are tested and compared. For a tool builder it is a real process to read, parse and run against: every view a commercial flow consumes exists here in open form.

## What the SKY130 kit contains

A PDK is the process described in files. SKY130 ships SPICE device models (for ngspice and Xyce), the layer definitions and design rules, DRC and LVS decks for open verifiers such as Magic, KLayout and Netgen, and libraries built on the process: standard cells, IO cells and some primitive devices. Each library cell comes in several views: a GDS layout, a LEF abstract, Liberty timing and power models per corner, a SPICE netlist and a Verilog model. What the PDK does not contain is anything specific to your design: RTL, SDC, floorplan choices and flow parameters are yours. When two people disagree about a DRC or timing result on the same layout, the first thing to compare is the PDK version, because rule decks, models and libraries evolve between releases. A flow that does not pin its PDK version is not reproducible.

## The SKY130 layer stack and libraries

SKY130 has a local-interconnect layer, li1, below five metal layers named met1 to met5. Standard cells use li1 for their internal wiring, which leaves more of met1 free for routing. Higher layers are thicker and less resistive, so they suit long wires and the power grid. Several standard-cell libraries share the process, named like sky130_fd_sc_hd: fd marking a foundry-provided library, sc for standard cell, and a suffix for the variant. hd is high density, hs is high speed, and there are others for low power, low leakage and different voltages. They trade cell height, transistor width and leakage, so the same RTL maps to different area and speed. A worked choice: a small controller with a relaxed 50 MHz clock and a tight area budget goes to hd. A datapath that misses timing at hd may close in hs, at the price of more area and leakage.

## How a flow consumes SKY130

Each flow stage reads the view it needs. Synthesis (Yosys and ABC) reads Liberty to know cell functions, area and delay. Placement and routing read the technology LEF (layers, vias, sites) and the cell LEF (size, pins, obstructions); they never touch transistor geometry. The static timer reads Liberty for the chosen corner, and extraction uses the layer stack to compute parasitics. At the end the flow replaces each LEF abstract with the cell's GDS (ORFS does this with KLayout), and the DRC and LVS decks check the merged layout. Two common mistakes come straight from this division. A final GDS with empty boxes where cells should be means the merge step did not run. Timing that looks too good often means a fast-corner Liberty was loaded, for example an ff file instead of tt, so every arc is faster than the corner you meant to sign off.

## Going deeper

The SkyWater SKY130 PDK documentation; the open_pdks installer documentation; the OpenROAD-flow-scripts platform files for sky130hd.

label: GF180MCU and IHP SG13G2
lesson:
# GF180MCU and IHP SG13G2

SKY130 is not the only open process. GF180MCU from GlobalFoundries and SG13G2 from IHP widen the choice: one aimed at mixed-voltage microcontroller-class designs, the other at SiGe BiCMOS for RF and high-speed analog. A tool builder who supports more than one PDK learns quickly which parts of a flow are process-neutral and which must be replaced, which is exactly the separation a good flow architecture enforces.

## GF180MCU for mixed-voltage designs

GF180MCU is a 180 nm process for microcontroller-class designs, released as an open PDK by GlobalFoundries. Its distinguishing trait is device options for several supply voltages, including higher-voltage devices useful for interfacing with 5 V signals, which the newer, thinner-oxide nodes cannot tolerate. It offers standard-cell libraries at more than one track height. Taller cells hold wider transistors and more internal routing room, so they drive larger loads and route more easily, but each cell costs more area. At 180 nm, digital density is low compared with modern nodes, so it suits control logic, sensor interfaces and mixed-signal glue rather than large datapaths. Moving a flow from SKY130 to GF180MCU breaks anything tied to the old site: row height, site name, tapcell spacing, PDN pitch and routing-layer names all change.

## IHP SG13G2 for SiGe BiCMOS and RF

IHP SG13G2 is a 130 nm SiGe BiCMOS process with an open PDK. BiCMOS means it offers both CMOS transistors and bipolar transistors on one die. The bipolar devices are silicon-germanium heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs), which switch far faster than the process's MOSFETs and are the reason the process exists: low-noise amplifiers, mixers, oscillators and high-speed drivers at frequencies well into the tens of gigahertz. Its metal stack includes thick top metals with low sheet resistance, which raise inductor quality factor and lower loss on RF lines and power routes. Because it is BiCMOS, it also has a CMOS standard-cell library, so a digital flow runs on it and RF and control logic can share a chip. The digital density is that of a 130 nm process, so a large digital block costs real area.

## Choosing and porting between open PDKs

Choose a PDK by its hardest requirement. Dense digital logic at modest speed: SKY130. Higher-voltage interfaces: GF180MCU. RF or very high-speed analog: SG13G2, accepting lower digital density. Then port the flow. Every physical and timing view comes from the PDK: technology LEF, cell LEF, Liberty per corner, cell GDS, SPICE models, and the DRC and LVS decks. On top of these, a flow keeps per-platform settings such as layer directions, PDN straps, tapcell rules, fill rules and the default routing layers. Well-structured flows keep these in a platform directory, separate from each design's configuration, which only names the platform. Then rerunning a design on another process is a one-line change in the design config, plus whatever the design itself must adapt to (a new clock target, a different IO ring).

label: What open access does not give you
lesson:
# What open access does not give you

Open PDKs and open tools let anyone design a chip and verify it. They do not, on their own, turn that design into a product. Knowing exactly where the open release stops matters for anyone who builds tools on it, because a tool that reports clean DRC or positive slack on an open PDK is reporting evidence under assumptions, not a guarantee of working, manufacturable, qualified silicon.

## What the open PDK files do not include

An open PDK releases rules, device models, layer data and basic libraries. It usually does not release the foundry's production yield data, statistical correlation between models and silicon lots, or a portfolio of complex, silicon-qualified IP: high-speed SerDes, PLLs, qualified SRAM compilers, and certified IO and ESD libraries. Some of these exist as open projects, for example open SRAM generators, but their models may not be validated across corners. Open DRC and LVS decks may also lag or simplify the foundry's internal signoff decks, so a layout clean under the open deck may still violate a rule the foundry checks. Treat open results as strong evidence within the encoded rules and models. When a design depends on something the release lacks, the risk is the designer's, and a tool should say which inputs were assumed.

## From open files to fabricated silicon

A verified GDS is not a chip. Mask making and wafer processing happen at a mask shop and the foundry, and they need a fabrication run. Open designs usually reach silicon through multi-project shuttles: many small designs share one mask set and one wafer run, which divides the dominant fixed cost, the masks, among all participants. Each project gets a handful of packaged or bare dies back. Prototypes that work at room temperature prove the design concept. A product still needs reliability qualification across temperature and voltage, a production test program, packaging qualification, and a supply agreement for volume. None of these comes from open files. A tool builder working on open flows should be clear that the flow ends at a verified handoff; the rest of the path is a business and engineering process with the foundry.

## Engineering around the gaps

Good practice on an open PDK is conservative. Reuse the IO cells the PDK provides rather than drawing new pad circuits, since ESD design depends on silicon data you do not have. Add timing margin beyond the reported slack: if the libraries have not been correlated to measured silicon, model error is unknown, and a guard band of a few percent of the clock period is cheap insurance. Choose modest clock targets and layouts that stay well inside the characterized range. Cross-check physical verification with two independent engines, such as Magic and KLayout. For research that should inform a commercial product, carry over methods and relative comparisons (algorithm A beats algorithm B by 4% wirelength on the same process) rather than absolute numbers, which do not transfer between processes and decks.

## Going deeper

The documentation of open shuttle programs and of the SKY130, GF180MCU and SG13G2 PDKs; Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), chapters on manufacturing and test.

label: Yosys and ABC in an open flow
lesson:
# Yosys and ABC in an open flow

Every open digital flow starts with Yosys, which reads Verilog, elaborates and optimizes it in its RTLIL intermediate representation, and hands the combinational logic to ABC for optimization and technology mapping against a Liberty library. A tool builder needs the script's structure, the exact handoff between the two tools, and the common failure signatures, because synthesis problems surface downstream as strange placement or timing.

## The shape of a Yosys synthesis script

A typical open-flow script reads the Verilog, then runs hierarchy with the top module named, which elaborates parameters and reports undefined modules. proc lowers always blocks into explicit multiplexers, flip-flops and latches. opt, fsm and memory passes simplify logic, extract and recode state machines, and map memories. techmap lowers generic cells into a fine-grained gate library. dfflibmap with the Liberty file maps the internal flip-flop cells onto real library flip-flops. abc with the Liberty file maps the remaining combinational logic. opt_clean removes dangling wires and cells, and write_verilog emits the structural netlist. Flows add passes for their downstream tools, such as tie-cell insertion for constants or buffer insertion for direct port-to-port assigns. Yosys also has a synth command that bundles a standard sequence; open flows usually write the steps out to control them.

## What ABC receives and returns

When Yosys runs abc, it extracts the combinational logic, writes it out for ABC, and reads the mapped result back, stitching it into the netlist between the flip-flops and other cells Yosys keeps. ABC represents logic internally as and-inverter graphs, optimizes them with rewriting, refactoring and balancing, then maps to the library using each cell's Boolean function, area and delay from the Liberty file. Geometry from LEF and clocks from SDC never enter. If a flow passes a clock period or delay target, ABC favors faster structures, often at more area; without one, it leans toward area. An example: a 32-bit adder mapped with no target tends toward a compact, slower structure; with an aggressive target ABC spends more cells to shorten the critical path, and the reported area rises.

## Diagnosing open synthesis failures

Three failures recur. First, "module not defined" for an SRAM or other hard macro: there is no RTL to synthesize, so the flow must supply a blackbox declaration or a Liberty model so Yosys keeps the instance as a black box. Second, a netlist far smaller than expected, with outputs tied to constants: logic that drives no observable output is legally removed, so an unconnected port, a typo in a port name or a missing keep attribute shows up as missing logic. Third, large area differences between two Liberty files from one PDK: mapping can only use the cells offered, so a library with richer complex gates or different sizes changes the result. A fourth, softer symptom is a netlist with plain assigns between ports that a physical tool rejects; flows insert buffers to give every connection a driving cell.

## Going deeper

The Yosys manual (passes proc, techmap, dfflibmap, abc); the ABC documentation and Mishchenko's papers on AIG rewriting and mapping; the OpenROAD-flow-scripts synthesis scripts.

label: The OpenROAD tool suite
prereqs: The RTL-to-GDSII flow end to end
lesson:
# The OpenROAD tool suite

OpenROAD is one application that links a set of physical-design tools onto one OpenDB database, driven from a Tcl shell or Python. Each tool has a short name and one job: initialize the floorplan, place pins, build the power grid, place cells, repair timing, build the clock tree, route, extract and time. Knowing which tool owns which job, and what it leaves in the database for the next, is the map a tool builder needs before modifying any of them.

## Floorplan and placement tools

ifp initializes the floorplan: it sets die and core areas, either explicitly or from a target utilization, and builds rows of sites from the library's site definition. ppl places top-level IO pins on the die boundary, usually to shorten wires to the cells they connect to. tapcell inserts well taps and endcaps that the process requires, and pdn builds the power distribution network of rings, straps and rails. gpl is the global placer, from the RePlAce line of electrostatics-based placers: it treats cells as charges, solves for a density potential, and moves cells with a Nesterov-type method toward low wirelength and uniform density. Its result still overlaps. dpl, the detailed placer, snaps every cell to a legal site in a row without overlap and makes local improvements. Each tool reads and writes the same database, so the next tool simply sees the updated objects.

## Optimization, clock and routing tools

rsz, the resizer, runs repair design (fixing maximum slew, capacitance and fanout by buffering and sizing) and repair timing (sizing and buffering to fix setup and hold). cts, from TritonCTS, builds a buffered clock tree toward balanced latency at the flip-flop clock pins. grt, the global router from the FastRoute line, divides the die into gcells, assigns each net a path through them and through layers, and reports congestion as demand versus capacity per gcell edge. It writes route guides. drt, from TritonRoute, turns guides into exact wires and vias that obey the design rules, iterating with rip-up and reroute and reporting any violations it cannot fix. Order matters: grt's guides confine drt's search, and the clock tree must exist before signal routing claims the tracks near the flip-flops.

## Extraction, timing and the shared database

OpenRCX extracts resistance and capacitance from the routed geometry using calibrated rules and writes them as SPEF or loads them for timing. OpenSTA is the static timer: it reads Liberty and SDC and times the design using estimated or extracted parasitics. Because all tools live in one process on one database, a tool can call another without writing a file. The resizer asks OpenSTA for slack after every batch of edits; a timing-driven gpl run asks for net criticality between iterations and reweights nets; global routing can feed estimated parasitics back to the timer. In a flow of separate point tools, each of those exchanges would be a DEF and SPEF write and read, minutes on a large design. This is why OpenROAD's architecture is a shared in-memory database with tools as modules, and why an incremental timer is part of it.

## Going deeper

The OpenROAD documentation for each tool (ifp, ppl, pdn, gpl, rsz, dpl, cts, grt, drt, OpenRCX, OpenSTA); Ajayi et al. on the OpenROAD project.

problems.e: ifp initializes the floorplan from a utilization or explicit die area and builds rows from the library site.

problems.e: gpl comes from the RePlAce line of electrostatics-based placers. Its output still has overlaps that legalization removes.

problems.q:

A) dpl, the detailed placer

problems.e: drt turns route guides into exact DRC-aware wires and vias and reports any violations it cannot fix.

problems.e: The resizer runs repair design and repair timing, sizing cells and inserting buffers.

problems.a: From grt to drt
problems.e: Global routing produces guides that confine the detailed router's search.

problems.e: Because tools share the database and process, the placer can ask the timer for criticality and reweight nets as it goes.
